# The robot

The `.core` file declares one robot: a chassis, and the parts placed on it.

```robotdsl
Robot diff_bot {
    intent "Two-wheel differential base with a rear caster and a top lidar"

    Diff_two_caster chassis(ref = "diff_base")
    Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
    Motor motor_r(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, -0.1, -0.02, 0, -1, 0))
    Standard wheel_l(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, 0.12, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
    Standard wheel_r(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, -0.12, -0.02, 0, -1, 0))
    Caster ball(ref = "caster_ball", glue = (-0.15, 0, -0.035, 0, 0, -1))
    Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06", glue = (0, 0, 0.06, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

Each line is a component: its type, its name, and its arguments. `intent` is an optional sentence for people and for the tools that generate programs.

## The chassis

Exactly one component is the chassis. Its type says how the robot drives, and its `ref` names the chassis part in a library:

```robotdsl
Diff_two_caster chassis(ref = "diff_base")
```

The chassis type decides which wheel mounts must be filled, which of them drive, and what the base can do:

| Chassis type | Wheels | Can spin in place | Holonomic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Diff_two_caster` | two `Standard`, plus a caster | yes | no |
| `Diff_drive` | four `Standard`, skid steer | yes | no |
| `Tracked` | two `Track`, skid steer | yes | no |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | four `Mecanum` | yes | yes |
| `Omni_drive` | four `Omni_wheel` | yes | yes |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | three `Omni_wheel` | yes | yes |
| `Tricycle` | one steered driven front wheel, two free rear wheels | no | no |
| `Ackermann` | two steered front wheels, driven or free, and two driven rear wheels | no | no |
| `Legged` | none: it stands on the feet of its legs, its own links or `Leg` parts placed on it, where their servos hold them | each way its gait turns | to each side its gait moves aside |

A `Legged` chassis is a part with legs of its own, or a body that carries legs: its file names the gait its walking controller takes and, when its legs are its own, the shapes of its links it stands on ([Component library format](../../reference/library.md#feet-and-gait)), and may state that controller, the policy or the gait its legs walk by ([Walking controller](../../reference/library.md#walking-controller)). A body's legs are `Leg` parts, each placed by glue where a hip goes; the chassis's gait walks them all ([Legs as parts](../../reference/library.md#legs-as-parts)), or a walker trained for that body on those legs, placed so, which the library registers, walks it, whatever the body states ([Walkers](../../reference/library.md#walkers)). The `mjcf` target writes a legged base by its controller or its walker; the ROS targets do not write one yet.

[Drive types](../advanced/drive-types.md) says what the compiler emits for each.

## Parts and glue

Every other component is a part placed by `glue`, or fastened through its holes ([below](#parts-fastened-through-their-holes)): the glue is the point and the direction of a connector, in the chassis frame. The connector is one of the chassis' own, or one of a part already placed: a wheel's glue is the end of its motor's shaft.

```robotdsl
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
Standard wheel_l(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, 0.12, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
//                                            x   y     z     nx ny nz
```

The glue must match one connector within 1 mm and 0.01 in direction; one that matches two is an error, and a part that mates onto that part is not placed either. The part's own connector is then mated to it, the two directions facing each other. A seventh number, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`, turns the part about the direction.

You do not have to look the values up. A glue that matches no connector is reported with the nearest one and the exact glue to write:

```text
error[validation.assembly.glue_on_connector]: the glue of 'wheel_lf' matches no connector of the chassis or of a placed part; the nearest is 'motor_lf.shaft', 0.008 m away with direction cosine 1.00
   --> demo.core:17:52
   |
17 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.12, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |                                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ matches no connector
   |
   = help: to mount on 'motor_lf.shaft' write glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0)
   = help: the free connectors are: chassis.front_mount, motor_lf.shaft
```

A connector holds one part. Every mount the chassis type drives carries one wheel of the right type: on the shaft of a `Motor` on the mount, which then bounds the wheel's speed and torque, or straight on the mount, driven within no stated limits when no motor is declared for it (a kit whose motors are built into its chassis). A wheel glued straight onto a mount the type does not drive rolls freely, such as a tricycle's rear wheels. See [Drive types](../advanced/drive-types.md#motors). A `Caster` is passive and may sit on any other connector.

## Parts fastened through their holes

A sensor, an `Attachment`, a `Mount`, a `Battery` or a `MotorDriver` whose part states the holes it is fastened by ([Interfaces](../../reference/library.md#interfaces)) may be fastened through them to the holes of another part, in place of a glue: `on` names that part, `at` its interface, `by` the part's own where its part states more than one, `offset_m` where on the other's pattern, `(u, v)` along its `up` and its `dir` x `up`, and `turn_rad` how it is turned about that interface's `dir`. With parts of the compiler's test library, a channel whose top is an 8 mm grid, an adapter from a 32 mm square to a Raspberry Pi 5's pattern, and a board on its threads:

```robotdsl
Attachment channel(ref = "channel_grid_8mm", glue = (0, 0, 0.06, 0, 0, 1))
Mount adapter(ref = "adapter_32_58x49", on = @core/channel, at = "top", by = "under_holes", offset_m = (0, 0.004))
Attachment board(ref = "board_58x49", on = @core/adapter, at = "board_holes")
```

The origin of the part's interface is put on the other's, moved by `offset_m`, the two faces against each other, and at `turn_rad = 0` the two interfaces' `up`s lie together. Its pose follows the part it is fastened to: written `offset_m = (0, 0.012)`, the adapter moves a grid step along and carries the board with it, the board's declaration unchanged, where a glue is a point in the chassis frame and would stay where it is written. A part states exactly one of `glue` and `on`. A wheel, a track, a motor and a leg are placed by glue alone.

Two faces that meet face each other, so a part's pattern is seen mirrored from the face it meets: a hole at `(u, v)` of its pattern, read from its own face, lands at `(u, -v)` on the other's, turned by `turn_rad`. A symmetric pattern is the same either way; a bracket whose three holes make an L lies on the grid as its part's frame draws it.

Where a part's holes meet the other's at more than one place at its turn, as a square on a grid nearly always does, `offset_m` says which: left out, the part is not placed, and the error lists the places they meet. They meet where each of the part's holes is joined to one of the other's within its play, as the fit below judges it, or overlaps one where a part states no screw that would decide: a plate whose holes lie 0.1 mm off the grid's lines meets it wherever it is centred on four of its holes, as one whose holes lie on them does. Where they meet at one place or none, `offset_m` may be left out and `(0, 0)` is judged. A turn is written in radians, and the grammar has no pi: a help prints a half turn as `3.14159265`, which moves a hole 0.2 m from the axis by less than a nanometre.

```text
error[validation.assembly.connection_placed]: 'adapter' fits 'top' of 'channel' at 4 offsets at turn_rad 0, and the program does not say which
   = help: write offset_m = (0, -0.012), (0, -0.004), (0, 0.004) or (0, 0.012) (4 offsets at turn_rad 0; the same 4 at turn_rad = 1.57079633, 3.14159265 or 4.71238898)
```

The compiler then pairs each of the part's holes with the hole of the other it lands on and judges whether a screw joins them, from the screw each interface states its holes are made for and whether they are threads for it. A screw passes a hole no narrower than itself, and a pair is joined when its axes lie within the play the two holes leave it, `(d1 - f)/2 + (d2 - f)/2`, within a micrometre. A thread is declared at its screw's size and holds that screw alone: a camera's 1/4-20 tripod socket on a 4 mm hole for M4 is refused, since the 6.35 mm screw its thread takes does not pass the hole, and so is a board's 2.7 mm holes on M3 threads; an M3 thread under a 4 mm hole for M4 is joined, with 0.5 mm of play. Where a part states no screw for its holes, they may be threads of their own size: a pair through them is joined only where their holes are the size of the screw the other states, or, neither stating one, where holes of one size lie on each other. Holes whose openings do not overlap are refused whatever the parts state, and the rest is a warning that names the fields to state:

```text
error[validation.assembly.holes_line_up]: the holes of 'plate' do not meet those of 'base': 'under_holes' spans 36 x 36 mm, 'top_holes' spans 32 x 32 mm
   = help: no offset_m or turn_rad puts the holes of 'under_holes' on those of 'top_holes': choose a part whose holes meet them, or join the two by an adapter
```

A hole that lands on two holes of the other alike, as near to each, is refused too, and a note names the two: judged at that distance, it fails as any pair that far off does, and otherwise which of the two takes the screw is not settled. A connection that fails for more than one reason names each in the same error. Each connection is judged on its own, so a plate whose holes miss leaves the result of the board on its other interface alone. Screws are not modelled: a part whose every hole is joined counts as fastened through its holes. A target holds a fastened part fixed to the part it is fastened to, as it holds a glued one ([Target output](../../reference/output.md)).

A hole takes the screw of one connection. Two parts fastened onto the same hole are refused at the later of the two in the program, the earlier named beside it, and so is a part fastened onto the holes its host is fastened by. A hole is one whatever interface names it: two interfaces of a part may both name it, as a grid and a square of four of its sites do, or name holes on one face with no wall between them, one opening, and either way it takes one screw. The help gives the nearest places where the later part's holes, or else the earlier's, meet none another part's screws take, or says that no place on the pattern frees them, as on a pattern that fits the part at one place only. Two plates of the test library written at one place on the channel's grid:

```robotdsl
Mount first(ref = "plate_32_m4", on = @core/channel, at = "top", offset_m = (0, 0.004))
Mount second(ref = "plate_32_m4", on = @core/channel, at = "top", offset_m = (0, 0.004))
```

```text
error[validation.assembly.one_fastener_per_hole]: 4 holes of 'channel' take the fasteners of both 'first' and 'second'
   = help: move 'second' to offset_m = (0, -0.004) or (0, 0.012) on 'top', where no hole it meets takes another's fastener
   = note: the holes of 'top' at (-0.016, -0.012), (-0.016, 0.02), (0.016, -0.012) and (0.016, 0.02)
```

What holds each placed payload is said too (`assembly.parts_held`): every component whose type supports `on`, even when its library part states no interfaces, and every part stored in a region. A part whose every hole is joined is held to the part it is fastened to, unless an earlier connection uses one of its holes or one screw would pass through it and two other parts, or the part it is fastened to is a [Mount](#mounts) that is not held itself. A part glued elsewhere than on a storage region's seat ([below](#parts-stored-in-a-region)) while its part lists holes on the face it is glued by is held by nothing the program states, so it is listed as undecided, without a warning, since a strap the builder adds may hold it: naming `on`, or, where other parts are fastened onto those holes, naming them with nothing to state. Its target's fixed joint is recorded in `compile.json` as standing in for what is missing ([What the compiler checks](../advanced/validation.md#does-each-part-stay-where-it-is-placed)). The adapter glued onto the channel's top in place of its connection, the board still on its threads, and the board listed too, since the adapter is a Mount that nothing holds:

```robotdsl
Mount adapter(ref = "adapter_32_58x49", glue = (0, 0, 0.108, 0, 0, 1))
```

```text
robot.core:9:5: undecided: adapter has no `on`: it is glued on channel.top_mount, and its part's interface under_holes joins nothing, so assembly.parts_held cannot be judged
robot.core:10:5: undecided: board is fastened to adapter, a Mount that is not held where it is, so assembly.parts_held cannot be judged
```

The connection above is the `on` it asks for. A glued payload without a usable interface remains undecided, naming the library part's `interfaces` instead of suggesting an `on` that cannot yet be written. Holes on another face, such as the threads the adapter offers the board, cannot establish the hold on this face. Neither a mesh that appears to touch the chassis nor a kit name establishes that hold. The unknown result allows draft compilation; choose a library adapter with both attachment sides stated, or obtain the missing part and interface description externally before claiming the assembly is supported.

Not in this version: one screw through three parts, which is refused as a hole two connections use; a hole used from both faces of a wall, which a part declares on each face as two holes, so that one screw through three parts there is not refused; a part fastened to two others; slots; a part other than a [Mount](#a-mount-fastened-by-its-grid) fastened by a grid of its own; and the strength of a joint, since no part states a load it takes.

## Parts stored in a region

A chassis, a `Mount` or an `Attachment` whose part states a storage region ([Storage regions](../../reference/library.md#storage-regions)) keeps a part in it, as a chassis keeps a pack in its battery compartment or a holder in its tray. A part is stored there when it is placed on the region's seat, a connector of that part: by a glue onto the seat, as a part is glued onto any connector, or with `on` naming the part and `at` the region, which seats it there by its `default` mount and carries it with its host. `turn_rad` turns it about the seat; `by` and `offset_m` place a part on a pattern of holes and are refused beside an ordinary whole-part region; partial capture selects its feature with `by` as described below. With the test library's holder, fastened to the channel by its square, and a pack in its tray:

```robotdsl
Attachment channel(ref = "channel_grid_8mm", glue = (0, 0, 0.06, 0, 0, 1))
Mount holder(ref = "holder_32_m4", on = @core/channel, at = "top", offset_m = (0, -0.012))
Battery pack(ref = "pack_76x46", on = @core/holder, at = "tray")
```

Written `offset_m = (0, 0.012)`, the holder moves 24 mm along the channel and carries the pack, whose declaration is unchanged; a pack glued onto the tray's seat would stay where its glue was written and match no connector.

The region is a void in its part's declared shape: a pack inside the box lies inside the holder's shape and crosses nothing, and one that crosses the shape outside the box is reported by `assembly.parts_clear_each_other`, by how deep it crosses there, with the size of the box a part stored there must fit, since a part on a seat is not moved by a distance. A stored part is held (`assembly.parts_held`) when every side of the region is closed, by a wall, a cover, a strap or an end stop, and its declared shape lies within the box, within 2 mm. Otherwise it is listed as undecided, without a warning: naming each side the region's part states `open`; with nothing to state where it reaches out of the box, since a shorter part is the change; or naming its part's `collision` where it declares none. An attachment of the test library, `bay_open_below`, whose compartment has no cover, the pack placed in it:

```text
test_parts/parts/bay_open_below/component.yaml:25:53: undecided: compartment of bay, where pack is stored, is open on -z, so assembly.parts_held cannot be judged
```

The line points at the side in the base's part file: a cover the base comes with would be stated there, `-z: cover`. A strap or a bracket the builder adds is stated nowhere, so a pack held so stays listed.

## Capturing part of a payload

A dock can retain a foot or a base without enclosing the whole arm. Its library
region states `capture: true`, and the arm names the physical feature under
`capture_features`. Select that feature explicitly:

```core
Attachment arm(ref = "robotdsl_drawing_arm_parked", on = @core/arm_dock,
    at = "base_capture", by = "base")
```

The feature's connector seats the arm and its feature box must fit the holder's
region. Positively closed sides establish geometric capture; an open or friction
side remains unknown. The dock itself must be held too. The rest of the arm is
still checked for interference, and the capture region does not erase holder
material. This establishes no clamp torque, strength or dynamic load rating.
See [Partial capture](../../reference/library.md#partial-capture) for declarations.

## Mounts

A part whose only job is to hold other parts, a plate, a bracket, an adapter, a standoff, a riser, a clamp or a holder, is a `Mount`, and its library entry's category is `mount` ([Mounts](../../reference/library.md#mounts)). It is placed as an `Attachment` is, by `glue` or with `on` through the holes its part lists, or [by a grid of its own](#a-mount-fastened-by-its-grid), and other parts are fastened to its holes or kept in its regions. With parts of the compiler's test library, a grid plate glued on the chassis's top connector and a body fastened to the plate's top by its four M3 threads:

```robotdsl
Mount deck(ref = "grid_plate_5x9", glue = (0, 0, 0.06, 0, 0, 1))
Attachment body(ref = "threads_32_m3", on = @core/deck, at = "top", offset_m = (0, 0))
```

A part fastened to a Mount, or kept in one, is held only where the Mount is: a Mount exists to carry what is on it to the robot, and a plate that nothing holds holds nothing. A Mount placed by glue is listed by `assembly.parts_held` as held by nothing stated, for want of `on`, and so is each part on it, naming the Mount, with nothing of its own to state; down a chain of Mounts each part names the Mount under it. Every other part's joint is judged on its own: a camera fastened to an arm is held to the arm, whatever holds the arm.

A Mount has no electrical role: `power`, `output`, `data`, `port`, `address`, `command` and `channel` are refused on it, since each part it holds names its own, and a `power`, a `data` or a motor driver's `command` that names a Mount is refused too. A part that holds others and has a job of its own besides, such as a pan-tilt head that turns what it holds on its servos, is an `Attachment`.

Three things to know before writing one:

- A set of standoffs or brackets used together is one Mount part in the library, stating every hole of the set, as the test library's `standoffs_m25` states its four threads. Four separate Mounts cannot carry one board, since a part is fastened `on` one other.
- A chain that stands for a part on two others, a tray on a bracket and a second bracket written `on` the tray to reach the chassis, compiles, but the second bracket's screws into the chassis are never judged and the chassis holes under it stay free for another part. Do not write it: a part fastened to two others is not in this version.
- A clamp, which grips a tube or an edge and states no holes, loads as a Mount and is placed by `glue`. A friction grip with no verified preload does not establish a hold; `assembly.parts_held` lists the clamp as held by nothing stated, naming its part's `interfaces`, and every part on it. A positively retained foot can use [partial capture](#capturing-part-of-a-payload), but that does not establish radial pin engagement or a friction grip.

### A Mount fastened by its grid

A Mount may be fastened by a grid of its own, as a goBILDA plate is screwed to a channel through whichever of its holes lie over the channel's: `by` names the grid, and `offset_m` and `turn_rad` place it as they place any part. Each site of the grid whose opening meets a hole of the host is judged as a hole is, and the others lie on the host's material or beyond it and fail nothing, since a plate is larger than the channel it lies on; a site off its hole's axis beyond the play, or on two holes alike, takes no screw and fails nothing either. The Mount is fastened where its sites are joined to two holes of the host or more: one screw would leave it free to turn about that screw, and two at two points do not. With the test library's grid plate on the channel's top:

```robotdsl
Mount deck(ref = "grid_plate_5x9", on = @core/channel, at = "top", by = "bottom", offset_m = (0, 0.004))
```

The evidence says the sites that meet holes, not the screws, since which of them take screws is the builder's choice at the bench: `28 sites on holes; a screw through any two of them fastens it`. For the same reason the Mount takes every hole of the host a site of it is joined to, or might be: a part fastened later through one of them is refused as a hole two connections use (`assembly.one_fastener_per_hole`), with a note naming the Mount. A grid that meets the host at one site only, or none, is refused, and the help names the nearest places where it is fastened:

```text
error[validation.assembly.holes_line_up]: no site of 'deck' meets a hole of 'top': its grid lies 4 mm off theirs
   = help: move it by offset_m to (0, 0.004) or (0.008, 0.004), where it is fastened
```

A grid fastened at more than one place at its turn, as one nearly always is, needs its `offset_m`; without it the Mount is not placed, and `assembly.connection_placed` lists the places at its turn and at the quarter turns, at which a square grid lies along a square grid of its pitch. Another turn, at which a few sites happen to meet holes, is judged where the program writes it and not offered. Where a part states no screw for its grid, whether its sites are joined is not settled, and the warning names the fields to state.

### A Mount across several interfaces

A Mount may be fastened across several interfaces of one part, as a plate is screwed to two cross channels of a chassis: `at` names them in one string, separated by commas, the first the one `offset_m` and `turn_rad` place it on. With one interface of its own in `by`, it is mated with all of them, which then lie on one plane, and its holes or its sites are paired with all of theirs at once, each pair judged with the screw its own host interface states. With the test library's frame, whose two tops lie 64 mm apart:

```robotdsl
Mount deck(ref = "grid_plate_5x9", on = @core/frame, at = "left_top, right_top", by = "bottom", offset_m = (0, 0.032))
```

Each interface `at` names must be met, by one joined hole or site at least: a Mount said to be fastened to one that it does not reach is refused, and the help names those it meets alone, or the nearest place where it meets every one. Interfaces that do not lie on one plane cannot take one face of the Mount, and it is not placed:

```text
error[validation.assembly.connection_placed]: 'right_top' and 'raised_top' of 'frame' do not lie on one plane (10 mm apart), so 'deck' cannot lie flat on both
   = help: name interfaces of one plane: left_top, right_top
```

A Mount that stands on two levels or two faces, as an adapter on a deck and on a box beside it, or an L-bracket, names as many interfaces of its own in `by`, each mated with the interface `at` names in the same place of its list:

```robotdsl
Mount step(ref = "stepped_adapter", on = @core/frame, at = "right_top, raised_top", by = "low_holes, high_holes", offset_m = (0, 0))
```

The first pair places it, and every other pair's faces must meet there, its holes on its host interface's plane and the two faces facing each other; otherwise the Mount is not placed, and the message says which face lies how far off which. Only a Mount is fastened across several interfaces, and it has one parent, the part `on` names, so the robot's description stays a tree; a part fastened to two other parts is not in this version.

A face that meets no hole of the interface it is paired with, or lies off that interface's plane, but rests on another interface of the part and meets its holes there, was named onto the wrong one, and the help writes `at` with that one in its place; otherwise it writes both lists without that pair. The adapter placed by its high foot on the raised top, its low foot named on the first top:

```robotdsl
Mount step(ref = "stepped_adapter", on = @core/frame, at = "raised_top, left_top", by = "high_holes, low_holes", offset_m = (0, 0))
```

```text
error[validation.assembly.holes_line_up]: no hole of 'step' meets a hole of 'left_top', though `at` names it; it meets 'raised_top' at 2 holes
   = help: name at = "raised_top, right_top", where 'low_holes' meets 2 holes of 'right_top', or at = "raised_top", by = "high_holes" alone
```

## Power and command

A chassis or `Leg` can use the same optional `power`, `output`, `data`, `port`
and `address` arguments as an attachment, where its library entry states the
corresponding external interfaces. A powered leg's accepted voltage is checked
against its named supply; a chassis with an Ethernet port can name its data
peer without declaring an external power input. These connections do not
describe internal batteries or controllers automatically. Leave unknown facts
unstated; `power_input: none` in the library means explicitly no power.

A power or a command connection is not a place, so it is not a glue but a reference to another component. A `MotorDriver` names what feeds it with `power`, and a `Motor` names the driver that drives it with `command`. A sensor and an `Attachment` name what feeds them with `power` too: a battery, or a part whose library entry states the outputs it feeds others from, such as a 5 V regulator or a computer's 5 V pins; where that part feeds others from more than one, `output` names which, `output = "3v3"`. The battery, the driver and the regulator are themselves parts glued onto connectors.

```robotdsl
Battery pack(ref = "lipo_3s_2200", glue = (-0.1, 0, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1))
MotorDriver driver(ref = "driver_vnh5019", glue = (0, 0.1, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/pack)
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0), command = @core/driver)
Attachment reg5(ref = "regulator_5v", glue = (-0.1, 0.08, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/pack)
Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06", glue = (0, 0.0001, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/reg5)
```

A motor like this one has two terminals, which go to one channel of its driver: the channel that commands it also powers it, so it names no `power`. A motor that carries its driver, a smart servo, is commanded over a bus and powered on a line of its own, and names both: `power = @core/pack, command = @core/board`.

A motor may name the channel it is on with `channel`: one its driver's part names, as the board prints it, `channel = "M1"` on the dual VNH5019, or, on a board whose part states only how many channels it has, a name of the program's own, which is compared and never read. Motors that name one channel turn together and draw from it together: a skid-steer base may put a side's two motors on one channel, and a mecanum base may not. A motor that names no channel is counted as needing one of its own.

Each part's supply is traced back to a battery, through every driver and regulator on the way: the lidar is fed the regulator's 5 V, and the regulator the pack's. From what the parts state, the compiler then checks that every part it can feed draws its power from a battery, that the driver, the regulator and the lidar each accept what they are fed, full and run down, that the motor's supply includes the voltage its ratings hold at, that one channel delivers the current the motor draws stalled, that a battery or a regulator that states the current it delivers delivers what the parts behind it draw, running and as the motors start, and that the driver has a channel, or speaks the bus, for each motor it commands. A sensor takes power unless its part says it takes none, as a bumper's switch does; an attachment takes power when its part states what it takes or feeds others from, or when it names a `power`. [Validation](../advanced/validation.md#does-every-part-get-its-power) lists the rules. A program that names no `power` and no `command` still compiles: the rules that would judge them are undecided, without a warning, and the check names each part that lacks one on a line above its summary ([What stays undecided](../advanced/validation.md#what-stays-undecided)):

```text
demo.core:12:5: undecided: motor_lf has no `command`, so command.driver_commands_its_motors, power.loads_fed_from_a_battery and power.rated_voltage_in_supply cannot be judged
```

## Links

A part that is read or commanded names what it is linked to, port to port, as it names its supply: a sensor or an `Attachment` with `data`, the computer or the board that reads it, and a `MotorDriver` with `command`, what commands it, as a motor names its driver. The ports are those its part and that part state ([Ports and buses](../../reference/library.md#ports-and-buses)), and the compiler joins the two that fit: a USB device and a USB host, an I²C target and an I²C controller, a UART and a UART, an Ethernet port and an Ethernet port, two ports on one bus. Where several ports of the part it names fit, `port` names which; and an I²C board that is not left at the address it is sold at says which of those its part states it is set to with `address`. On a computer whose part states two USB host ports and an I²C controller, `computer_5v` of the compiler's test library, two IMUs of one kind, a camera and a motor controller of the same library are linked so:

```robotdsl
IMU imu_front(ref = "imu_i2c", glue = (0.06, 0, 0.03, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/computer, output = "3v3", data = @core/computer)
IMU imu_rear(ref = "imu_i2c", glue = (-0.06, 0, 0.03, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/computer, output = "3v3", data = @core/computer, address = "0x6a")
Camera camera(ref = "camera_usb", glue = (0.12, 0, 0.03, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/computer, output = "5v", data = @core/computer, port = "usb3_0")
MotorDriver controller(ref = "motor_controller_i2c", glue = (-0.12, 0, 0.03, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/pack, command = @core/computer)
```

The camera names one of the two USB ports; the IMUs and the motor controller share the one I²C bus and name no port. Left at the address they are sold at, the two IMUs would answer together, so the rear one is set to the other address its part states. The compiler checks that the ports of each link fit, that no port carries more links than it takes, and that no two boards on an I²C bus answer at one address ([Validation](../advanced/validation.md#is-every-motor-commanded-and-every-link-joined)). A part that is read and names no `data` still compiles: the link rules list it on a line above the summary, as they list a part that names no supply.

## Component types

| Kind | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Motors | `Motor`: on a drive mount, with the wheel it drives on its shaft; `command` names its driver, and `channel` the channel it is on |
| Power | `Battery`: a pack on any free connector. `MotorDriver`: a board on any free connector; `power` names what feeds it, and `command` what commands it |
| Wheels | `Standard`, `Mecanum`, `Omni_wheel`, `Caster` |
| Legs | `Leg`: a leg of its own, on servos, ending in the feet it stands on, placed on a `Legged` chassis that has no legs of its own |
| Tracks | `Track`: a belt with its sprockets and road wheels as one part, where a `Tracked` chassis has a wheel's place |
| Sensors | `Lidar`, `Lidar3D`, `Camera`, `DepthCamera`, `RGBD`, `IMU`, `Ultrasonic`, `Range`, `Bumper` |
| Mounts | `Mount`: a plate, a bracket, an adapter, a standoff, a riser, a clamp, a holder; it holds other parts and has no electrical role |
| Other | `Attachment`: an arm, a gripper, a tray, a computer, a regulator; it adds mass and shape, and is fed and feeds others where its library entry states what it takes and what it feeds others from, and is linked to others by the ports its entry states |

A part can be used as a type when its library entry lists that type. The [vocabulary](../../reference/vocabulary.md) lists every type with what it means.

## Names

Component names are how the task and the evaluation refer to parts: `@core/wheel_l`. Two components cannot share a name, and the names of the links the targets add are reserved: `base_footprint`, `base_link`, `<link>_contact_<n>` for a ground contact a part declares, and `<wheel>_steer` for a steered wheel's knuckle.

## Next

[The world](./world.md) places the robot among obstacles and goals.

pages.title: The world
pages.text:
# The world

The `.world` file declares where the robot starts, what surrounds it, and the places the task refers to.

```robotdsl
World demo {
    physics(gravity = (0, 0, -9.81))
    spawn(robot = @core/diff_bot, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
        Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5))
        Marker flag(type = "cylinder", pos = (2.5, 0, 0.01, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.02))
    }
    Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

## Poses

A pose is seven numbers, a position and a quaternion: `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`. No rotation is `(x, y, z, 0, 0, 0, 1)`. Lengths are metres.

## Physics and spawn

`physics(gravity = (x, y, z))` sets gravity in m/s². Without it, the targets use standard gravity, `(0, 0, -9.81)`.

`spawn` places the robot the `.core` file declares:

```robotdsl
spawn(robot = @core/diff_bot, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
```

## Scenarios and entities

A scenario groups the things in one environment. Its `ref` is the base environment: `"empty"` for none, where the room is whatever the scenario's entities make it, or the id of an environment a library holds, [below](#environments-from-a-library). `ground_plane = true` adds a floor, and without one the robot falls.

Each entity has a type, a name, a shape and a pose:

| Entity type | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `Obstacle` | Something the robot must not touch. Touching one fails the run's physical verdict. |
| `SupportSurface` | A floor, ramp or pad the robot drives on; contact is expected. |
| `Marker` | A visual mark, such as a goal disc. It has no collision unless `collision = true`. |

The shape is a `type` of `"box"`, `"sphere"` or `"cylinder"` with a `size` of `(x, y, z)` in metres; a sphere's diameter and a cylinder's are the `x` size, a cylinder's height the `z` size. Or the entity is an object of a library, named by `ref`, as the next section says.

Entities stay where they are placed. Leave `is_static` out, or write `is_static = true`; the two ROS targets refuse an entity declared movable, because an entity states no mass to move it with.

Obstacles are drawn into the navigation map, seen by the robot's sensors, and measured against when a run is judged. The compiler measures against them too, before anything runs: a world that spawns the robot with a part in an obstacle is refused, and a place the task navigates to where the robot cannot stand is warned of ([What the compiler checks](../advanced/validation.md#can-the-base-make-the-motions-the-task-asks-for)).

A `Marker` that does not collide is only seen. Both simulators' cameras see it. Gazebo's lasers and range finders see it too, since they see what is shown; MuJoCo's return only from what collides, which `compile.json` says for each such mark.

A program states no light and no colours. Both simulators light a world alike: a sun, a pale sky, a light grey floor, and a mid grey for a shape a program states. A colour camera reads one world in the two within a few parts in 255. A camera draws nothing beyond the far end of its range and shows the sky there: 5 m from it for one that measures depth, 10 m ahead of it for a plain one.

An entity's name is its own, apart from the robot's components. The Gazebo target holds the robot and the floor as models of the same world, so there an entity cannot share the robot's name, or `ground_plane` when the scenario has a floor.

## Objects from a library

A table, a shelf or a ramp is not written as boxes. It is an object of a [component library](./libraries.md#objects-for-the-world), and an entity takes it by its id, as a component takes its part:

```robotdsl
Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
    Obstacle table(ref = "work_table", pos = (2.0, 0.6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    SupportSurface ramp(ref = "ramp_10deg", pos = (1.0, -1.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Marker spot(ref = "floor_disc", pos = (3.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

The example library holds a pallet rack, a work table, a pallet jack, a cardboard box, a traffic cone and a pallet, each a model that a collection publishes for simulators, and a ramp and a mark painted on the floor.

The object's library entry states the mesh it is shown by and the shapes it collides by. The program states where it stands, by `pos`, and what it is to the robot, by the entity type: the same crate is an `Obstacle` in one world and a `Marker` in another. A program names no file and no address; where an object's mesh comes from is its library's business.

An entity takes `type` with `size`, or `ref`: never both, and never `size` beside `ref`, since an object is as large as its entry says. An object that declares no collision is only shown, so it can be a `Marker` and cannot be an `Obstacle` or a `SupportSurface`.

The map and the run's verdict take an object by its shapes, each where it stands: a gate by its two posts and not by the passage between them. They take each shape seen from above, as they take a primitive, so a table's top covers the floor under it and a robot is planned around the table, not under it.

Both simulators show an object's mesh to their cameras, in its materials' colours and with the pictures laid on them. Gazebo decodes the mesh, and its lasers see it too. MuJoCo decodes no glTF, so the output's own node reads the mesh, while its lasers see the shapes the object collides by; `compile.json` says so for each object. A laser sees a ramp as it sees a wall, so a robot that navigates by a laser does not plan a way up one.

## Environments from a library

A room or a hall is written once, in a [component library](./libraries.md#objects-for-the-world), and a scenario takes it whole by its id:

```robotdsl
Scenario room(ref = "room_6x4") {
    Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5))
}
Goal goal(target = @world/dock)
```

The environment brings its floor and its entities: here a storeroom of four walls, with a loaded pallet rack, a work table, a pallet with two cartons, a pallet jack, a traffic cone and a mark on the floor called `dock`. They are the scenario's own beside the ones the program adds: drawn into the map, seen by the sensors, judged against, and named like any entity, so a goal can target the room's `dock` and a task drive to it. An entity the program adds cannot take a name the environment already holds.

An environment that brings its floor needs no `ground_plane`. A world has one floor: `ground_plane = true` is refused as a second where an environment of any of the world's scenarios brings its floor, or where another scenario already lays it. The floors of two environments are that one floor. An environment's entities stand where its library entry places them, in the world's frame; a scenario does not move or turn the environment it takes.

## Goals

A goal is a named place the task can drive to, given by a `pose` or by an entity as `target`:

```robotdsl
Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
Goal at_flag(target = @world/flag)
```

The task refers to it as `@world/goal`.

## Next

[The task](./task.md) says what the robot does in this world.

pages.title: The task
pages.text:
# The task

The `.task` file is what the robot must do, as a behavior tree: actions such as `Navigate` and `Spin`, arranged by control nodes such as `Sequence` and `Retry`.

```robotdsl
Task drone_demo(timeout_s = 120) {
    Retry(count = 2) {
        Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
    }
    Sequence {
        Spin(angle_rad = 1.57),
        Wait(duration_s = 2),
        Stop()
    }
}
```

The nodes in the task's body run in order. `timeout_s` bounds the whole task; when it runs out, the run ends with status `timeout`.

## Actions

| Action | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `Navigate(goal = @world/...)` | Drive to a goal or an entity, avoiding obstacles |
| `Spin(angle_rad = ...)` | Turn in place by a signed angle |
| `Advance(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive straight ahead; the speed is optional |
| `BackUp(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive straight back |
| `Strafe(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive sideways, positive to the left |
| `Wait(duration_s = ...)` | Do nothing for a while |
| `Stop()` | Come to rest |

An action with no arguments keeps its parentheses, `Stop()`, so two nodes in a row never read as one.

## Control flow

| Node | Runs its children |
| --- | --- |
| `Sequence { ... }` | In order, stopping at the first failure |
| `Fallback { ... }` | In order, stopping at the first success |
| `Parallel(policy = "success_on_all") { ... }` | Together; `"success_on_one"` succeeds when any child does |
| `Retry(count = n) { ... }` | Its one child again until it succeeds, at most `n` times |
| `Repeat(count = n) { ... }` | Its one child `n` times |
| `Timeout(timeout_s = t) { ... }` | Its one child, failing it after `t` seconds |
| `Inverter { ... }` | Its one child, swapping success and failure |

Conditions are leaves that succeed or fail without moving: `GoalReached(goal = ...)`, `DistanceTraveled(distance_m = ...)` and `TimeExpired(duration_s = ...)`.

```robotdsl
Task deliver(timeout_s = 180) {
    Fallback {
        GoalReached(goal = @world/goal),
        Retry(count = 3) {
            Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
        }
    }
    Stop()
}
```

## What, not how

The task names what the robot must accomplish, not how a navigation stack does it. There is no node for a planner, a controller or a costmap, and no syntax to pick one; the target binds each action to its stack. [The output contract](../../reference/output.md#the-task) lists what each action becomes.

The base has to be able to do what the task asks. `Spin` needs a base that turns in place, and `Strafe` a holonomic one; a tricycle asked to spin is an error at compile time, not a surprise in the simulator.

## Next

[The evaluation](./evaluation.md) says how a run of this task is judged.

pages.title: The evaluation
pages.text:
# The evaluation

The `.eval` file is optional. It lists checks, each a measurement of the run with bounds it must stay within.

```robotdsl
Evaluate demo_eval {
    Check_clearance(target = @world/goal, min = 0.3)
    Check_vel(target = @core/wheel_lf, min = 0, max = 60)
    Check_time(target = @task/drone_demo, max = 300)
}
```

Every check takes at least one of `min` and `max`, and every check but `Check_clearance` a `target`.

## Checks

| Check | Measures | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Check_vel` | A joint's speed, rad/s, every sample | a wheel, `@core/...` |
| `Check_acc` | A joint's acceleration, rad/s², every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_jerk` | A joint's jerk, rad/s³, every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_effort` | A joint's effort, N·m, every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_distance` | Distance to a goal or entity: `min` bounds the closest approach, `max` the distance at the end | `@world/...` |
| `Check_clearance` | The closest approach to an obstacle over the run | `@world/...`, or every obstacle |
| `Check_contact` | Seconds a part spends touching a scene entity | a part, `@core/...` |
| `Check_time` | The task's duration, seconds | `@task/...` |

`Check_distance` and `Check_clearance` also take a `source`, the part measured from; without it they measure from the whole robot. On a `Bumper`, `Check_contact` reads what the bumper itself reported; on any other part, the simulator's geometry.

## How checks are judged

A check is judged from the simulator's own record of the run, never from what the robot or its navigation stack believed: the robot's pose as the simulator publishes it, the joint states, and the bumpers' reports. Each check ends `pass`, `fail` or `unknown`. A check with no samples to judge is `unknown`, never `pass`.

A joint check on a part that has no moving joint is refused at compile time, since there would be nothing to measure.

The checks are one of three verdicts a run gets; [Judging a run](../advanced/judging-a-run.md) explains the other two.

## Next

[Component libraries](./libraries.md) explains where the parts come from.

pages.text:
# Vocabulary

This page is generated from `mobiledsl.semantic.model.vocabulary`; edit the code,
not the page. It lists every name a program may use beyond the grammar's
keywords, and what each takes. Numbers carry no unit: the parameter name carries
it by suffix (`_s` seconds, `_m` metres, `_rad` radians, `_mps` metres per second).

## Component types (`.core`)

A component type is the kind of part a program places. A part can be used as a
type when its library entry lists the type under `profiles`; the type's category
is the kind of physical thing the part must be, which decides what its entry
declares (a wheel its radius, a chassis its connectors). A chassis takes `ref`
and optional external power/link arguments; a wheel, track, motor and leg are placed
by `glue`, and a sensor, an
attachment, a mount, a battery and a motor driver by `glue` or by `on`, through the
holes its part states or in a storage region of the part it is put on. A type exists
only when the compiler acts on it: a chassis type has kinematics, a wheel type a
contact model, a track type a belt the targets stand in for, a sensor type a simulated
sensor and a use for its data, a motor ratings that bound its wheel, a battery and a
motor driver ratings the power and command rules judge, and a mount the grid it is
fastened by, the interfaces of one part it spans, the refusal of any power or link and
the hold it passes on to what it holds.
A part that only holds others is a `Mount`.
A part no other type names is an `Attachment`. What the compiler does with one
beyond carrying it, its library entry's blocks say, not a type name: the power it
takes, the outputs it feeds other parts from, and the ports it is linked by; the entry
also says what the part is.

| Type | Category | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | chassis | Four mecanum wheels; holonomic. |
| `Diff_drive` | chassis | Four driven standard wheels, skid steer. |
| `Diff_two_caster` | chassis | Two driven standard wheels and a caster. |
| `Tricycle` | chassis | One steered, driven front wheel and two free rear wheels. |
| `Ackermann` | chassis | Two steered front wheels, two driven rear wheels; the front wheels may be driven too. |
| `Omni_drive` | chassis | Four omni wheels; holonomic. |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | chassis | Three omni wheels on a circle; holonomic. |
| `Tracked` | chassis | Two tracks, each driven on its own; skid steer. |
| `Legged` | chassis | Legs on servos, its own or Leg parts placed on it; stands on their feet, walks as its gait states. |
| `Mecanum` | wheel | A mecanum wheel. |
| `Standard` | wheel | A plain driven wheel. |
| `Caster` | wheel | A passive support wheel. |
| `Omni_wheel` | wheel | An omni wheel. |
| `Track` | track | A track as one part: a belt around its sprockets and road wheels. It mates by the hub that drives it and moves the base by the travel its part states per turn. |
| `Motor` | motor | A motor on a drive mount of the chassis, where the wheel glued onto its shaft is driven, or on a seat of the chassis whose driveline turns the wheels of other mounts; within the speed and torque its part states. Its `command` names the motor driver that drives it, and `channel` the channel it is on. |
| `Battery` | battery | A battery pack, placed as a sensor or an attachment is; the parts whose `power` names it run on the voltage its part states. |
| `MotorDriver` | motor_driver | A board that drives motors: each motor without a bus from a channel of its own, within the current its part states, and motors that carry their driver over a bus it speaks. Its `command` names what commands it. |
| `Lidar` | sensor | A planar laser scanner. |
| `Lidar3D` | sensor | A spinning multi-ring laser; its cloud marks obstacles and its middle ring can stand in for a planar laser. |
| `Camera` | sensor | An RGB camera. |
| `DepthCamera` | sensor | A depth camera; its cloud can stand in for a laser. |
| `RGBD` | sensor | A colour camera with a registered depth image; its cloud can stand in for a laser. |
| `IMU` | sensor | An inertial measurement unit. |
| `Ultrasonic` | sensor | A range finder that measures with sound in a narrow cone; its reading marks the costmaps' range layer. |
| `Range` | sensor | A range finder that measures with light (infrared or time of flight) in a narrow cone; its part states its range, cone and rate, and its reading marks the costmaps' range layer. |
| `Bumper` | sensor | A contact switch on the body; Check_contact on it reads what pressed it. |
| `Attachment` | attachment | A part no other type names: an arm, a gripper, a tray, a computer, a regulator. It adds mass and shape, and takes power, feeds other parts from its outputs or is linked to other parts by its ports where its library entry says so; the library entry says what it is. |
| `Mount` | mount | A part whose only job is to hold other parts of the robot: a plate, a bracket, an adapter, a standoff, a riser, a clamp, a holder. A set used together, such as four standoffs under one board, is one part. It adds mass and shape and has no electrical role: it takes no power, feeds no other part and is linked to none. It may be fastened by a grid of its own, wherever two of its sites or more are joined to the holes of the part it is fastened to, and across several interfaces of that part. What is fastened to it, or kept in it, is held only where it is. |
| `Leg` | leg | A leg of a Legged chassis that has none of its own: links on hinges its servos turn, ending in the feet it stands on; the chassis's gait walks it with the others. |

Parameters of a chassis:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or part that delivers power>` | no | What the part draws its power from: a battery, or a part that feeds others from the outputs its library entry states, such as a regulator or a computer's 5 V pins. |
| `output` | string | no | Which output of the part `power` names it draws from, where that part feeds others from more than one. |
| `data` | `@core/<sensor, attachment, chassis, leg or motor driver>` | no | What the part is linked to, a port of its own joined to one of that part's: the computer or the board that reads it, or that it reads. |
| `port` | string | no | Which port of the part `data` names the link joins, where several of that part's ports fit one of its own. |
| `address` | string | no | The address an I²C target is set to, such as "0x6a", among those its part states it may be set to; without it, it answers at the address it is sold at. |

Parameters of a wheel or track:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |

Parameters of a leg:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or part that delivers power>` | no | What the part draws its power from: a battery, or a part that feeds others from the outputs its library entry states, such as a regulator or a computer's 5 V pins. |
| `output` | string | no | Which output of the part `power` names it draws from, where that part feeds others from more than one. |
| `data` | `@core/<sensor, attachment, chassis, leg or motor driver>` | no | What the part is linked to, a port of its own joined to one of that part's: the computer or the board that reads it, or that it reads. |
| `port` | string | no | Which port of the part `data` names the link joins, where several of that part's ports fit one of its own. |
| `address` | string | no | The address an I²C target is set to, such as "0x6a", among those its part states it may be set to; without it, it answers at the address it is sold at. |

Parameters of a battery:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | no | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. A part states exactly one of `glue` and `on`. |
| `on` | `@core/<component>` | no | The part it is fastened to through its holes, or kept in, in place of `glue`: the chassis or a part placed on it, whose library entry states the interface or the storage region `at` names. Moving that part moves this one. |
| `at` | string | no | Which interface of the part `on` names it is fastened to, or which storage region of it it is kept in, seated on the region's seat, by its name in that part. |
| `by` | string | no | Which interface of its own part it is fastened by, where its part states more than one: one that lists its holes, not a grid. For a capture region, the required name of its capture feature. Not beside an ordinary whole-part storage region. |
| `offset_m` | tuple of 2 | no | Where the origin of its interface sits on the pattern `at` names, `(u, v)` along that interface's `up` and its `dir` x `up`; (0, 0) when left out. Required where its holes meet that pattern at more than one place at its turn, each joined to one within its play or, where a part states no screw, overlapping one. Not beside a storage region. |
| `turn_rad` | number | no | How far it is turned about the `dir` of the interface `at` names, or of a storage region's seat, counter-clockwise seen from where that `dir` points, from the turn at which the two `up`s lie together; 0 when left out. |

Parameters of a sensor or an attachment:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |

| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | no | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. A part states exactly one of `glue` and `on`. |
| `on` | `@core/<component>` | no | The part it is fastened to through its holes, or kept in, in place of `glue`: the chassis or a part placed on it, whose library entry states the interface or the storage region `at` names. Moving that part moves this one. |
| `at` | string | no | Which interface of the part `on` names it is fastened to, or which storage region of it it is kept in, seated on the region's seat, by its name in that part. |
| `by` | string | no | Which interface of its own part it is fastened by, where its part states more than one: one that lists its holes, not a grid. For a capture region, the required name of its capture feature. Not beside an ordinary whole-part storage region. |
| `offset_m` | tuple of 2 | no | Where the origin of its interface sits on the pattern `at` names, `(u, v)` along that interface's `up` and its `dir` x `up`; (0, 0) when left out. Required where its holes meet that pattern at more than one place at its turn, each joined to one within its play or, where a part states no screw, overlapping one. Not beside a storage region. |
| `turn_rad` | number | no | How far it is turned about the `dir` of the interface `at` names, or of a storage region's seat, counter-clockwise seen from where that `dir` points, from the turn at which the two `up`s lie together; 0 when left out. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or part that delivers power>` | no | What the part draws its power from: a battery, or a part that feeds others from the outputs its library entry states, such as a regulator or a computer's 5 V pins. |
| `output` | string | no | Which output of the part `power` names it draws from, where that part feeds others from more than one. |
| `data` | `@core/<sensor, attachment, chassis, leg or motor driver>` | no | What the part is linked to, a port of its own joined to one of that part's: the computer or the board that reads it, or that it reads. |
| `port` | string | no | Which port of the part `data` names the link joins, where several of that part's ports fit one of its own. |
| `address` | string | no | The address an I²C target is set to, such as "0x6a", among those its part states it may be set to; without it, it answers at the address it is sold at. |

Parameters of a mount:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | no | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. A part states exactly one of `glue` and `on`. |
| `on` | `@core/<component>` | no | The part it is fastened to through its holes, or kept in, in place of `glue`: the chassis or a part placed on it, whose library entry states the interface or the storage region `at` names. Moving that part moves this one. |
| `at` | string | no | Which interface of the part `on` names it is fastened to, or which storage region of it it is kept in, seated on the region's seat, by its name in that part; or several interfaces of that part, their names separated by commas, "middle_top, front_top", the first the one `offset_m` and `turn_rad` are measured on, each met by one of its holes or sites at least. |
| `by` | string | no | Which interface of its own part it is fastened by, where its part states more than one: one that lists its holes, or a grid, whose sites joined to the holes `at` names fasten it wherever two of them or more are. Where `at` names several: one interface, mated with all of them, which then lie on one plane; or as many, separated by commas, each mated with one of them in order, for a Mount that stands on two levels or two faces. Not beside a storage region. |
| `offset_m` | tuple of 2 | no | Where the origin of its interface sits on the pattern `at` names, the first where it names several, `(u, v)` along that interface's `up` and its `dir` x `up`; (0, 0) when left out. Required where it is fastened there at more than one place at its turn: its listed holes each joined to one within its play, or, where a part states no screw, overlapping one; or two of its grid's sites or more so joined. Not beside a storage region. |
| `turn_rad` | number | no | How far it is turned about the `dir` of the interface `at` names, the first where it names several, or of a storage region's seat, counter-clockwise seen from where that `dir` points, from the turn at which the two `up`s lie together; 0 when left out. |

Parameters of a motor:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or part that delivers power>` | no | What the motor draws its power from. A motor without a bus is powered through the driver that commands it and needs no `power` beside `command`; one with a bus names its supply here: a battery, a motor driver, or a part that feeds others from the outputs its library entry states. |
| `output` | string | no | Which output of the part `power` names a motor with a bus draws from: where that part feeds others from more than one, and always where it is a motor driver that states outputs. A motor without a bus names none: the channel that commands it powers it. |
| `command` | `@core/<motor driver>` | no | The motor driver that commands the motor: from one of its channels, or over the motor's bus. |
| `channel` | string | no | Which channel of the driver `command` names the motor is on: one its part names, as its board prints it, or, where its part states only how many it has, a name of the program's own. Motors that name one channel turn together and draw from it together; a motor that names none is counted as needing one of its own. |

Parameters of a motor driver:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | no | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. A part states exactly one of `glue` and `on`. |
| `on` | `@core/<component>` | no | The part it is fastened to through its holes, or kept in, in place of `glue`: the chassis or a part placed on it, whose library entry states the interface or the storage region `at` names. Moving that part moves this one. |
| `at` | string | no | Which interface of the part `on` names it is fastened to, or which storage region of it it is kept in, seated on the region's seat, by its name in that part. |
| `by` | string | no | Which interface of its own part it is fastened by, where its part states more than one: one that lists its holes, not a grid. For a capture region, the required name of its capture feature. Not beside an ordinary whole-part storage region. |
| `offset_m` | tuple of 2 | no | Where the origin of its interface sits on the pattern `at` names, `(u, v)` along that interface's `up` and its `dir` x `up`; (0, 0) when left out. Required where its holes meet that pattern at more than one place at its turn, each joined to one within its play or, where a part states no screw, overlapping one. Not beside a storage region. |
| `turn_rad` | number | no | How far it is turned about the `dir` of the interface `at` names, or of a storage region's seat, counter-clockwise seen from where that `dir` points, from the turn at which the two `up`s lie together; 0 when left out. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or part that delivers power>` | no | What the part draws its power from: a battery, or a part that feeds others from the outputs its library entry states, such as a regulator or a computer's 5 V pins. |
| `output` | string | no | Which output of the part `power` names it draws from, where that part feeds others from more than one. |
| `command` | `@core/<sensor, attachment, chassis, leg or motor driver>` | no | What commands the board, a port of its own joined to one of that part's: the computer or the controller board it takes its commands from. |
| `port` | string | no | Which port of the part `command` names the link joins, where several of that part's ports fit one of its own. |
| `address` | string | no | The address an I²C target is set to, such as "0x6a", among those its part states it may be set to; without it, it answers at the address it is sold at. |

### Chassis types

What each chassis type needs and what the assembled base can do. A mount is
driven in one of three ways. A `Motor` sits on it, its `glue` equal to the chassis
connector that the part's profile maps the mount to, with one wheel of an allowed
type on the motor's shaft. Or the wheel sits on the mount itself and a `Motor`
sits on a connector of the chassis whose `driveline` turns that mount. Or the wheel
sits on a mount the type always drives and no motor is declared: the kit's motors
are then part of its chassis, and the targets drive the wheel within no stated
limits and say so. On a mount that does not drive, or on an optional mount with
no motor, the wheel sits alone and rolls freely. A `Caster` wheel is
passive and may sit on any other connector. Every mount is driven unless the
table lists the driven ones; a mount listed as optional is driven or free, together
with the others listed so. One motor turns one mount, or through a driveline one
of the sets under shared drive. A mount that steers turns about the kingpin the
chassis part declares on that connector. A `Tracked` base carries a `Track` where
the others carry a wheel, on its two mounts, and they are driven the same two ways.
A `Legged` base carries neither: its legs are its part's own links, or `Leg` parts
placed on it when it has none of its own. It stands on their feet, where their servos
hold them, and its part's `gait` says what its walking controller takes: it moves
aside when the gait takes a speed aside, and turns in place when the gait takes a turn.

| Chassis | Wheel mounts | Wheel type | Driven | Shared drive | Steered | Holonomic | Spins in place |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Mecanum` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Diff_drive` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | all | `front_left_wheel` + `rear_left_wheel`; `front_right_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel` | none | no | yes |
| `Diff_two_caster` | `left_wheel`, `right_wheel` | `Standard` | all | none | none | no | yes |
| `Tricycle` | `front_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | `front_wheel` | none | `front_wheel` | no | no |
| `Ackermann` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel`; optional: `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel` | `rear_left_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel`; `front_left_wheel` + `front_right_wheel`; `front_left_wheel` + `front_right_wheel` + `rear_left_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel` | no | no |
| `Omni_drive` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Omni_wheel` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | `front_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Omni_wheel` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Tracked` | `left_track`, `right_track` | `Track` | all | none | none | no | yes |
| `Legged` | none: it stands on its feet | none | none | none | none | its gait's | its gait's |

## World (`.world`)

### Entity types

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Obstacle` | Something the robot must not touch: touching it fails the run. |
| `SupportSurface` | A floor, ramp or pad the robot drives on; contact is expected. |
| `Marker` | A visual mark such as a line or a goal disc; no collision by default. |

All entity types take the same parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `box`, `sphere`, `cylinder` | no | A primitive shape; exactly one of `type` and `ref`. |
| `ref` | string | no | The id of a library object, shown by its mesh and colliding by the shapes its entry declares; exactly one of `type` and `ref`. |
| `pos` | tuple of 7 | yes | World pose `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`; no rotation is `(x, y, z, 0, 0, 0, 1)`. |
| `size` | tuple of 3 | no | Primitive dimensions `(x, y, z)` in metres; required with `type`, refused with `ref`. |
| `is_static` | bool | no | Fixed in place (default `true`). No target moves an entity: it states no mass to move it with, so `false` is refused. |
| `collision` | bool | no | Emits collision geometry (default depends on the type). An object that declares no collision cannot collide. |

### `Scenario`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The base environment: the id of a library environment, whose floor and entities the scenario takes, or `empty` for none. |
| `ground_plane` | bool | no | Lay the world's ground plane (default `false`). A world has one: this is refused where an environment of any of its scenarios brings its floor, or another scenario already lays it. |

### `Goal`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pose` | tuple of 7 | no | The goal pose `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`; one of `pose` and `target`. |
| `target` | `@world/<entity>` | no | An entity whose pose is the goal; one of `pose` and `target`. |

### `physics`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gravity` | tuple of 3 | no | Gravity `(x, y, z)` in m/s^2. |

### `spawn`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `robot` | `@core/<robot>` | yes | The robot declared in the `.core` file. |
| `pose` | tuple of 7 | yes | Where the robot starts, `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`. |

## Task (`.task`)

### `Task`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | The whole task must finish within this many seconds. |

### Composites (take children)

#### `Sequence`

Run children in order; stop at the first failure.

No parameters.

#### `Fallback`

Run children in order; stop at the first success.

No parameters.

#### `Parallel`

Run children together.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `policy` | `success_on_all`, `success_on_one` | yes | When the parallel succeeds. |

### Decorators (take exactly one child)

#### `Retry`

Re-run the child until it succeeds, at most `count` times.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | number | yes | Number of attempts. |

#### `Repeat`

Run the child `count` times.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | number | yes | Number of attempts. |

#### `Timeout`

Fail the child if it runs longer than `timeout_s`.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

#### `Inverter`

Swap the child's success and failure.

No parameters.

### Actions

#### `Navigate`

Drive to a goal, avoiding obstacles.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `goal` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | A goal or an entity in the world. |

#### `Wait`

Do nothing for a while.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `duration_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

#### `Stop`

Come to rest.

No parameters.

#### `Spin`

Turn in place.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `angle_rad` | number | yes | Signed angle in radians. |

#### `Advance`

Drive straight ahead.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

#### `BackUp`

Drive straight back.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

#### `Strafe`

Drive sideways; needs a holonomic base.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Signed distance in metres; positive is left. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

### Conditions

#### `GoalReached`

True when the robot is at the goal.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `goal` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | A goal or an entity in the world. |

#### `DistanceTraveled`

True once the robot has moved this far.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |

#### `TimeExpired`

True once this much time has passed.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `duration_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

## Evaluate (`.eval`)

### `Check_vel`

Joint speed in rad/s: the magnitude of every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_acc`

Joint acceleration in rad/s^2, the difference of successive speed samples; every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_jerk`

Joint jerk in rad/s^3, the second difference of the speed samples; every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_effort`

Joint effort in N*m: the magnitude of every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_distance`

Distance in metres from the robot (or `source`) to `target`: `min` bounds the closest approach over the run, `max` the distance when the task ends. The robot is measured from its recorded position, a part from a point of its own shape seen from above, its declared ground contacts aside: the middle of the rectangle around its box or hull, square to the chassis; the centre of a wheel; the middle of a track's run on the ground where the track declares no shape; the part's origin where it declares no collision.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | The entity or goal measured to. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_clearance`

Distance in metres from the robot (or `source`) to the nearest obstacle, at its closest over the run.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | no | The obstacle to measure to; every obstacle when absent or not an obstacle. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_contact`

Seconds the robot part `target` spends touching a scene entity: what its contact switch reports when it is a Bumper, else the simulator's geometry.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The robot part. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_time`

Duration of the task in seconds, from its first tick to its last.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@task/<task>` | yes | The task. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |
