# Grammar

A program is four files: the robot (`.core`), the world (`.world`), the task
(`.task`), and optionally the evaluation (`.eval`). Each file holds exactly one
declaration of its kind. The files are given to the compiler on the command
line, and the extension says which form a file is. There is no project
manifest: the target, the component libraries, and the output directory are
compile-time settings, so they are command-line options, not something the
author writes next to the program.

The grammar fixes the statement forms and nothing else. Component types, world
entity types, task node types, and check names are ordinary names that later
phases resolve against the standard vocabulary, the component libraries, and
the target. A file that names a component or an action the compiler has never
seen is syntactically valid; whether the name exists is decided by name
resolution, not here. Adding vocabulary never changes the grammar.

The normative grammar is `src/mobiledsl/frontend/grammar/robotdsl.lark`, read
by Lark with the LALR algorithm and a contextual lexer. The test suite builds
every start rule in strict mode, so no two terminals can match the same text.
When this page and the file disagree, the file is right and this page has a
bug.

## Common forms

Every declaration is a keyword, a name, and a braced body. Inside a body,
items have one of two shapes:

```text
Type name(parameter = value, ...)          a named item of some type
keyword(parameter = value, ...)            a setting with no name
```

Arguments are always named. Items may be separated by commas, by line breaks,
or by both, and a trailing comma is allowed. Comments are `//` to end of line
and `/* ... */`; block comments do not nest. Line endings may be LF or CRLF.

### Values

| Value | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| string | double quotes, JSON escapes | `"mecanum_black"`, `"a \"quoted\" word"` |
| number | optional sign, decimal, optional exponent | `2`, `-0.0216`, `1.5e-1` |
| boolean | `true`, `false` | `is_static = true` |
| tuple | two or more numbers in parentheses | `(0, 0, -9.81)`, `(2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)` |
| reference | `@namespace/name` | `@core/wheel_lf`, `@world/goal`, `@task/drone_demo` |

Numbers carry no unit; the parameter name does, by suffix: `timeout_s`,
`distance_m`, `angle_rad`. A tuple's meaning (a pose of seven numbers, a size
of three, a glue of six or seven) is decided by the parameter that takes it,
not by the grammar. The reference namespaces are `core`, `world`, and `task`;
any other namespace is a diagnostic, but the tree is still built. Identifiers
are `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`.

## CoreDSL (`.core`)

```text
robot_decl: "Robot" NAME "{" intent? component* "}"
intent:     "intent" STRING
component:  NAME NAME params
```

The first name of a component is its type, the second its instance name.
`intent` is a sentence for people and for the tools that generate programs; it
comes before the components.

```text
Robot drone_mecanum {
    intent "Drone mecanum mobile base with four black mecanum wheels and a top lidar"

    Mecanum_four_wheel chassis(ref = "tslot_1515_drone")
    Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
    Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06", glue = (0, 0.0001, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

## WorldDSL (`.world`)

```text
world_decl: "World" NAME "{" world_item* "}"
world_item: physics | spawn | scenario | goal
physics:    "physics" params
spawn:      "spawn" params
scenario:   "Scenario" NAME params "{" entity* "}"
entity:     NAME NAME params
goal:       "Goal" NAME params
```

`physics` and `spawn` are settings of the world and have no name. A scenario
groups the entities of one environment; each entity has a type (for example
`Obstacle`, `SupportSurface`, `Marker`) and a name that tasks and checks refer
to as `@world/<name>`. A goal is a named location.

```text
World demo {
    physics(gravity = (0, 0, -9.81))
    spawn(robot = @core/drone_mecanum, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
        Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5), is_static = true)
    }
    Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

## TaskDSL (`.task`)

```text
task_decl: "Task" NAME params? "{" node* "}"
node:      NAME params block?
         | NAME block
block:     "{" node* "}"
```

A node is a type followed by arguments, a block of children, or both. Which
types take children (`Sequence`, `Fallback`, `Retry`, ...) and which are
actions (`Navigate`, `Spin`, `Wait`, ...) is vocabulary, not grammar. A leaf
keeps its parentheses even when it has no arguments, `Stop()`, so that two
nodes in a row never read as one.

The task vocabulary names what the robot must accomplish. It does not name
how a target accomplishes it: there is no node for a navigation stack's
planner, controller, or costmap, and no syntax to select one. Those choices
belong to the target and its configuration.

```text
Task drone_demo(timeout_s = 120) {
    Retry(count = 2) {
        Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
    }
    Sequence {
        Spin(angle_rad = 1.57),
        Wait(duration_s = 2),
        Stop()
    }
}
```

## EvaluateDSL (`.eval`)

```text
eval_decl: "Evaluate" NAME "{" check* "}"
check:     NAME params
```

```text
Evaluate demo_eval {
    Check_clearance(target = @world/goal, min = 0.3)
    Check_vel(target = @core/wheel_lf, min = 0, max = 60)
    Check_time(target = @task/drone_demo, max = 300)
}
```

## Accepted and rejected

Accepted:

| Source | Why it is interesting |
| --- | --- |
| `Robot r {}` | the smallest declaration of each kind is valid |
| `Robot r { Hovercraft body(ref = "x") }` | unknown vocabulary is a name-resolution question |
| `Task t { Dock(station = @world/dock) }` | so are actions the compiler has never seen |
| `Robot r { A a(ref = "1"), B b(ref = "2"), }` | commas are optional, a trailing one is fine |
| `Task t { Sequence { } Stop() Retry(count = 2) { Stop() } }` | block only, arguments only, both |
| `Task t { Spin(angle_rad = -1.5e-1) }` | signs and exponents |
| `// line` `/* block */` | both comment styles |

Rejected, with the diagnostic it produces:

| Source | Diagnostic |
| --- | --- |
| `World w {}` in a `.core` file | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'World'; expected 'Robot' |
| `Robot a {} Robot b {}` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'Robot'; expected end of file |
| `Lidar l("lidar_ld06")` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: expected one of ')', a name — arguments are named |
| `Stop Wait(duration_s = 1)` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'Wait'; expected one of '(', '{' |
| `Goal g(pose = (1))` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected ')'; expected ',' — a tuple has two or more numbers |
| `Robot r {} # comment` | `syntax.unexpected_character`: `#` comments are gone |
| `/* a /* b */ c */` | `syntax.unexpected_token` at `c` — block comments do not nest |
| `Robot r {` | `syntax.unexpected_eof`: expected one of 'intent', '}', a name |
| `Robotarm {}` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'Robotarm'; expected 'Robot' — a keyword is a whole word |
| `Navigate(goal = @wrold/goal)` | `syntax.unknown_reference_namespace` |
| `Lidar l(ref = "a", ref = "b")` | `syntax.duplicate_parameter`, pointing at both occurrences |

The diagnostics are specified in [Diagnostics](diagnostics.md).

## Changes from the previous compiler

The previous compiler's four grammars are the starting point. What changed,
and why:

- Component types, task node types, and check names were grammar keywords
  (21, 15, and 9 of them). They are names now, so a new sensor, action, or
  check is a vocabulary entry, not a grammar change, and the task language is
  no longer tied to one navigation stack's node set.
- Poses, vectors, and references were strings: `glue="0.1275 0.1494 ..."`,
  `goal="@world/goal"`. They are tuples and references now, so the parser
  checks them and every number has its own span.
- `spawn { "@core/x": "pose" }` is `spawn(robot = @core/x, pose = (...))`, and
  `physics { gravity="..." }` is `physics(gravity = (...))`, the same shape as
  every other setting.
- `ComputePathToPose`, `FollowPath`, `path="{path}"`, `ClearLocalCostmap`,
  `ClearGlobalCostmap`, `controller=`, `planner=`, `PipelineSequence`, and
  `TransformAvailable` are gone from the task language: they described the
  navigation stack, not the task.
- `tick_rate_hz` on `Task` is gone: the previous compiler accepted it and
  never used it.
- `#` comments are gone; `/* */` comments are new.

## What the grammar leaves to later phases

- Whether a name exists and what it is.
- Which parameters a type takes, their types, units, and tuple lengths.
- Whether a reference resolves, and whether its namespace fits the parameter.
- Which node types take children, and whether a task or a robot is complete.
- Whether the target supports an action.

# Component library format

A component library is a directory the compiler is given with `--library`. It
holds the physical parts a program assembles a robot from, the objects a
world places and the environments a scenario takes. The compiler reads
two kinds of file from it, `library.yaml` and each part's `component.yaml`,
and checks that the assets they name exist. It never opens a mesh, and it
never reads the catalog, archive, or generated pages that a library
repository may keep beside them. There is no install step and no default
location.

This page is the schema. The library repository documents how parts are
built; the compiler is the only implementation of what a declaration means.

## Layout

```text
<library>/
├── library.yaml                     name and the registered ids: parts, objects, environments, walkers
├── parts/<part-id>/
│   ├── component.yaml               the declaration specified here
│   ├── assets/                      the mesh the declaration names, and what that mesh keeps beside it
│   └── ...                          README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG, images, source: not read
└── walkers/<walker-id>/
    ├── walker.yaml                  a walker's declaration (see Walkers)
    └── assets/                      its policy
```

### `library.yaml`

```yaml
name: demo_parts          # an identifier
parts:                    # each id is parts/<id>/component.yaml
  - tslot_1515_drone
  - mecanum_black
walkers:                  # optional; each id is walkers/<id>/walker.yaml
  - quad_walker
```

A part that is not listed does not exist to the compiler. An id listed twice
or without a declaration is a diagnostic; the other parts still load. An
[object](#objects) and an [environment](#environments) are listed and laid out
as a part is; its `category` says which an entry is, so an id names one thing.
A [walker](#walkers) is listed under `walkers` and laid out in `walkers/`.

## `component.yaml`

Values are YAML, read as JSON: only `true` and `false` are booleans, `null`,
`~` and an empty value are null, and a plain scalar is a number when it spells a JSON number
(`1e-3` is a number here, unlike in YAML 1.1). A key given twice is a
diagnostic. A key the schema does not list is a diagnostic; there are no
free-form fields, except inside `provenance`, where unknown keys are ignored.

Every length is in metres, every angle in radians, every mass in kilograms,
and every vector is `[x, y, z]` in the part's own frame: `+X` forward, `+Y`
left, `+Z` up. Every number is 0 or between 1e-100 and 1e30 in size, judged as
the float it reads as: no quantity of a part is smaller or larger, and what
the targets work out from such a number can overflow or be lost to zero. A
zero that a computation left a rounding off, such as -2.7e-32, is within it; a
number written nearer zero than any float, such as 1e-400, reads as 0 but is
no zero, and is not. Nothing is defaulted. A value the declaration does not
state is absent, and a later phase that needs it reports what is missing
rather than assuming.

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: mecanum_black                    # equals the directory name
category: wheel                      # what the part is; see Fields
description: Black 97 mm mecanum wheel.

visual:                              # the mesh that is shown
  file: assets/model.dae             # relative to the part directory
  xyz: [-0.0002, 0, -0.001]          # where the mesh sits in the part frame
  rpy: [0, 0, 1.57079]

wheel:                               # wheels only, and required for them
  radius: 0.0487                     # across the axle
  width: 0.0479                      # along the axle

inertial:
  mass: 0.09643
  origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0]              # centre of mass
  inertia: {ixx: 7.5613e-05, ixy: 0, ixz: 0, iyy: 7.5613e-05, iyz: 0, izz: 0.000114351}
  source: estimated                  # measured | datasheet | cad_measured | estimated | placeholder
  basis: solid cylinder at 270 kg/m^3   # how an estimate was chosen; required for estimated and placeholder

connectors:                          # mating points, at least one
  mount:
    pos: [-0.0013, 0.0011, 0]
    dir: [0, 0, 1]                   # mating axis, unit length
    joint: {type: continuous, axis: [0, 0, 1]}   # the joint created when mated; fixed when absent

profiles:                            # the component types the part can be used as
  Mecanum:
    mounts: {default: mount}         # logical mount name -> connector
```

### Fields

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | yes | `1` |
| `id` | yes | The part id; must equal the directory name |
| `category` | yes | `chassis`, `wheel`, `track`, `sensor`, `attachment`, `mount`, `leg`, `motor`, `battery`, or `motor_driver` for a part of a robot ([Mounts](#mounts)); `object` for a thing a world places and `environment` for a place a scenario takes, which state the fields under [Objects](#objects) and [Environments](#environments) and not these |
| `description` | yes | One sentence for people |
| `visual` | yes | `file`, `xyz`, `rpy`. `file` is a relative path to a mesh that exists, in a directory of its own inside the part directory, conventionally `assets/`, and not beside the declaration. That directory goes into an output whole: a mesh may keep what it is made of in other files, a glTF its buffers and textures, an OBJ its materials, and names them by relative path, and the compiler opens no mesh to learn which. So what a mesh names lies in that directory or below it, and nothing else is kept there; each of those files is the part's own, not a link out of the part directory |
| `collision` | no; not for wheels | `type: box` with `size` (three positive numbers) and `origin_xyz`, or `type: hull` with `vertices` (at least four `[x, y, z]` points) and `faces` (triangles as three indices into the vertices, wound either way) that bound a convex solid: a corner more than 1 µm outside a face's plane is refused, and so are triangles that do not close one solid of some volume, every edge bordering exactly two of them and none naming a corner twice or given twice. Or `type: compound` with `boxes`, one to 128 explicit material boxes, each with `size` and `origin_xyz`; boxes may overlap and gaps stay empty. Stands in for the mesh in collision checks and in the simulators, where a hull is written as a binary STL and each compound box as a separate collision shape. Without it the mesh is the collision shape |
| `wheel` | wheels only, required | `radius`, `width`, both positive. A wheel's rolling contact is derived from these, so a wheel declares no `collision` |
| `track` | a `Track` part, required; no other part | A track's belt, from its maker's data: `travel_per_turn_m`, how far the belt travels per turn of the hub the part mates by (positive), when the maker's data gives it; `width` (positive); and `ground: {from: [x, y, z], to: [x, y, z]}`, the two ends of the belt's run on the ground in the part frame, which may not be one point. The travel is stated and not a radius: a link tread moves its sprocket's teeth times its links' pitch per turn, less than the sprocket's outline gives. Without it `kinematics.tracks_state_their_travel` cannot decide and no target drives the base. A track may declare a `collision` box around its whole unit, for the footprint; in the simulators it collides through a box on its belt's run |
| `inertial` | yes | `mass` (positive), `origin_xyz`, `inertia` (all six terms; `ixx`, `iyy`, `izz` positive, and the principal moments, which the products `ixy`, `ixz`, `iyz` turn the diagonal into, positive and each at most the sum of the other two, judged in exact arithmetic on the numbers as stated, allowing for their rounding to the nearest doubles, 5 × 2⁻⁵³ of the largest entry: a thin plate stated in round decimals on the edge passes, and a tensor beyond it by more does not; a part's own tensor, which the MuJoCo targets hand on as it is stated, is held as MuJoCo holds it too, its two lesser principal moments adding up in floats to at least the largest, and a link's, which the `mjcf` target writes within the inequality, is not), `source`, `basis`, and optional `scope` (`base` by default, or `assembly` for an articulated product's aggregate at its declared static configuration) |
| `connectors` | yes, non-empty | Named mating points, below |
| `profiles` | yes | The component types the part can be used as, below. A part with `profiles: {}` is a catalog entry that no program can select |
| `motor` | a `Motor` part, required; no other part | What the motor's datasheet states: `rated_voltage_v`, the voltage its ratings hold at, and at that voltage `no_load_speed_rad_s`, `stall_torque_nm` and `stall_current_a` (its output shaft's speed unloaded, its torque stalled and the current it then draws), all positive. The wheel on its shaft turns within that speed and torque. `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, the supply it accepts, only when its maker states them: both or neither, the minimum not negative, the rated voltage between them. `bus`, a name, when the motor carries its driver and is commanded over that bus |
| `battery` | a `Battery` part, required; no other part | What the battery's page states: `voltage_nominal_v`, the voltage it is sold by when stated (positive); `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, what it delivers run down and full, both or neither, both positive and the nominal between them; `capacity_ah` (positive) when stated. At least one battery rating is required; capacity alone is valid and implies no nominal voltage or cell count. A pack that states no voltage range leaves the voltage rules undecided. `continuous_current_a`, the current it delivers continuously, as its maker or its protection circuit states it, when stated, and beside it `peak_current_a`, what it delivers for a moment, when stated: positive, the peak not below the continuous. A pack that states no current is not judged by the current rules |
| `driver` | a `MotorDriver` part, required; no other part | What the board's datasheet states. `channels`, the motors it drives from outputs of its own: how many, a positive integer, or their names as the board prints them beside their terminals, `[M1, M2]`, each once, a name of digits quoted, `["1", "2"]`; with it, required, `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v` (the motor supply it accepts, the minimum not negative) and `continuous_current_per_channel_a`, and `peak_current_per_channel_a` when stated, not below the continuous. `buses`, a list of names: the buses it commands motors over that carry their driver. A board states `channels`, `buses`, or both; one with `buses` alone may state its supply range. `output_voltage_v` when it regulates what it feeds its motors and does not pass its supply on, and beside it `efficiency`, the fraction of the power it takes for them that it delivers, when stated: above 0 and at most 1, the least where its maker gives a range. With `channels`, `continuous_current_total_a` and `peak_current_total_a` when its maker states what its channels deliver together below what they deliver each: positive, the peak not below the continuous |
| `power_input` | a sensor's, an attachment's, a chassis's or a leg's, optional; a motor driver's, optional, with its own current bounds alone; no other part's | What the part takes for its power, as its maker states it: `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, the supply it accepts, both or neither, the minimum not negative and at most the maximum; `voltage_nominal_v`, the one voltage it is sold for, positive and within that range when one is stated; and `continuous_current_a`, the most it draws continuously itself, beside what its outputs deliver, not negative: a regulator board's quiescent current. Optional `startup_current_a` independently bounds its own power-on current, also nonnegative. A motor driver states its supply in its `driver` block, and here only what it draws itself. Or the plain `none`: the part takes no power, a switch its host reads. [Power inputs and outputs](#power-inputs-and-outputs) |
| `power_outputs` | a sensor's, an attachment's, a chassis's, a leg's, a motor driver's or a motor with a `bus`'s, optional | The outputs the part feeds other parts from, each by a name of letters, digits and underscores as its board prints it (`5v`, `3v3`, `out`): at the voltage it is sold by, `voltage_nominal_v` (positive), and, when its maker states them, `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, the least and the most it delivers (both or neither, positive, the nominal between them); or `passes_input: true`, passing on what the part is fed, with no voltage of its own. Either may state `continuous_current_a`, what it delivers continuously, and beside it `peak_current_a`, what it delivers for a moment (positive, the peak not below the continuous), and one at a voltage of its own its `efficiency`, as a driver does. [Power inputs and outputs](#power-inputs-and-outputs) |
| `ports` | a sensor's, an attachment's, a chassis's, a leg's or a motor driver's, optional | The ports the part is commanded or read by, or commands and reads others by, one for each socket, each by a name of letters, digits and underscores as its board prints it (`usb3_0`, `i2c1`): its `kind`, `usb`, `i2c`, `uart`, `ethernet` or `bus`; its `role`, `host` or `device` for USB and `controller` or `target` for I²C, required for both and refused on any other kind; `bus`, the name of a port of kind `bus`, letters, digits and underscores; and an I²C target's `address`, as sold, and `addresses`, what else it may be set to. A motor driver states the buses it speaks in its `driver` block and no `bus` port. [Ports and buses](#ports-and-buses) |
| `range` | a `Range` part, required; an `Ultrasonic` part, optional; no other part | What a range finder measures, from its datasheet: `min_m` (not negative), `max_m` (positive, at least `min_m`), `field_of_view_rad` (the full cone about `+x`, positive and below pi) and `rate_hz` (positive). Equal `min_m` and `max_m` make a fixed-distance sensor, which says only whether something is within that distance. The part's frame is the sensor's emitter: its origin where the beam starts, `+x` along it |
| `contacts` | no | A list of `{xyz, radius, note}`: molded ground contacts of a chassis, such as a skid or a ball, as spheres. The statics rule counts each one that reaches the wheels' plane, and the targets simulate each as a sphere that slides |
| `interfaces` | a chassis's, an attachment's, a mount's, a sensor's, a battery's or a motor driver's, optional | The holes the part is fastened by, each group on one face, [below](#interfaces) |
| `capture_features` | optional | Named local portions held by a capture region: each has a `connector` and a positive `box` (`size`, `origin_xyz`) within the part's declared outer collision shape. The portion must describe a physical foot, flange or other retained feature, not an arbitrary point selected to fit a holder. [Partial capture](#partial-capture) |
| `storage` | a chassis's, a mount's or an attachment's, optional | The regions it keeps other parts in, each a box, the connector a kept part is seated on and what closes each side, [below](#storage-regions) |
| `links` | a leg's, required; a chassis's or an attachment's, optional; no other part's | The bodies the part moves below its frame, [below](#links) |
| `provenance` | no | `name`, `manufacturer`, `source_url`, `license`; each a string or `null`. `license` is an SPDX expression when known. Any other key here is ignored: a library may keep what its own tools need (a price, a maker's catalog number) with the part, and the compiler never sees it. A key given twice here, as anywhere in the file, still leaves the part out |

### Connectors

A connector is where another part mates. `pos` is the mating point, `dir`
the mating axis: a wheel's axle, a mount's normal. It points out of the part,
toward what mates there: up from a deck, down from the underside a board sits
on. Two parts mate with their `dir` vectors anti-parallel and their `pos`
points coincident, so a part whose connector points into it is turned over on
a connector that points out. `up`, when
given, fixes the roll about `dir` for a part whose orientation matters (a
camera lens, a lidar scan plane, a deck); it must be a unit vector
perpendicular to `dir`. A rotation-symmetric part states no `up`.

`joint` is the joint that mating this connector creates: `{type: fixed}` (the
default), or `continuous`, `revolute`, or `prismatic` with a unit `axis`. A
wheel's axle connector carries `continuous`; a chassis mount carries nothing.
Only a wheel turns on its connector. The targets refuse a moving joint on a
connector a mating uses (`target.unsupported`): on the mating part's own
connector unless the part is a wheel, and on the connector it mates onto
whatever mates there. A connector no mating uses is not checked. A chassis, an
attachment or a leg moves bodies of its own through `links`.

`well`, when given, is the void inside the part's collision box that what mates on
this connector may fill: `{radius: 0.052, width: 0.084}` is a cylinder about the
connector's axis, centred on it. A box is a bound drawn around the whole part, so a
kit's chassis box covers the arches its wheels turn in and a motor's box the hub its
wheel sits against; the clearance rules let a part into the declared shape exactly as
far as a well on the connector it mates by, or mates onto, holds, and no further. A
compartment that keeps a part is a [storage region](#storage-regions) instead, whose
seat states no well.

`steering` is stated by a chassis on a wheel mount that steers:
`{axis: [0, 0, 1], max_angle_rad: 0.6}` is the kingpin's axis in the part
frame and how far the wheel turns each way. Only a chassis may state it, and
the connector of every mount its chassis type steers must. The compiler
articulates the kingpin; the steering actuator and the knuckle body are the
target's.

`driveline` is stated by a chassis on a connector where a motor seats to turn
wheels that sit on other connectors, through shafts and gears of the chassis'
own: `{turns: [hub_rear_left, hub_rear_right], reduction: 2.33}` names the
connectors whose wheels the motor turns, and how many turns of the motor's
shaft make one turn of theirs. A car's axle with one motor and a differential
is the case. `reduction` is stated when the maker's data gives it; without it
the targets leave those wheels' joints without limits and say so. Only a
chassis may state a driveline, each connector it names once, and none of them
a connector that states a driveline itself. Which wheels one motor may turn
together is vocabulary, as is which mounts drive.

### Interfaces

A part may state the holes it is fastened by, beside its connectors.
`interfaces` maps a name, an identifier that is not the name of one of the
part's connectors or storage regions, to a group of round holes on one face of
the part. A
Raspberry Pi 5's four mounting holes, as measured in its maker's STEP file:

```yaml
interfaces:
  mounting_holes:
    pos: [0, 0, 0.00019]             # the face's origin: the board's underside
    dir: [0, 0, -1]                  # out of the face the holes open on, toward what mates
    up: [1, 0, 0]                    # the pattern's u axis; its v axis is dir x up
    fastener_diameter: 0.0025        # the screw the holes are made for: M2.5
    threaded: false                  # the screw passes them; they are not threads for it
    holes:
      - {at: [-0.029, -0.0245, 0.00019], diameter: 0.0027}
      - {at: [-0.029, 0.0245, 0.00019], diameter: 0.0027}
      - {at: [0.029, -0.0245, 0.00019], diameter: 0.0027}
      - {at: [0.029, 0.0245, 0.00019], diameter: 0.0027}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pos` | yes | The face's origin, a point on it, in the part frame |
| `dir` | yes | A unit vector out of the face the holes open on, toward what mates, as a connector's `dir`: two interfaces mate with their `dir`s anti-parallel |
| `up` | yes | A unit vector perpendicular to `dir`, the pattern's u axis, which fixes how the pattern is turned as a connector's `up` does. Its v axis is `dir` x `up` |
| `fastener_diameter` | with `threaded` | The nominal diameter of the screw the holes are made for, as its maker states it: 0.004 for M4. Stated with `threaded` when the maker states it, and otherwise neither |
| `threaded` | with `fastener_diameter` | `true` when the holes are threads for that screw, which hold it and no other, as a standoff's M2.5 thread or a camera's 1/4-20 tripod socket does; `false` when the screw passes them |
| `holes` | one of `holes` and `grid` | The holes, at least one, each `{at: [x, y, z], diameter}`: its centre on the face, in the part frame, and its diameter; a thread's is its screw's |
| `grid` | one of `holes` and `grid` | Holes on a lattice, [below](#grids) |

Every centre lies on the face, the plane through `pos` square to `dir`. A
thread is declared at its screw's diameter, and nothing else tells it from a
clearance hole of that diameter, so `threaded` is never defaulted: the
interface states it beside the screw, or states neither. A clearance hole is no
narrower than its screw, and a thread is its screw's size. No two holes of an
interface meet: two holes with no wall between them are one opening, a slot,
which this version does not declare. Lengths within 1 µm of each other are one
length: a library states lengths to 0.1 mm or finer.

A chassis, an attachment, a mount, a sensor, a battery or a motor driver may
state interfaces; a wheel, a track, a motor and a leg may not, since their
mounts carry the drive. A program fastens a sensor, an attachment, a mount, a
battery or a motor driver through its interface to another part's with `on`,
in place of a glue, and the compiler judges whether a screw the two state
joins each pair of holes
([The robot](../guide/basics/robot.md#parts-fastened-through-their-holes)).
A part may be fastened by an interface that lists its holes, and to any
interface, a grid's too; a mount may be fastened by a grid of its own too
([A Mount fastened by its grid](../guide/basics/robot.md#a-mount-fastened-by-its-grid)). Two interfaces of a part may name the same hole, as a
grid and a square of four of its sites do, or holes on one face whose openings
meet: either is one hole, and the compiler refuses two connections that use it
(`assembly.one_fastener_per_hole`). A hole a screw may pass from either face of
a wall may be declared on each face, as a rail that is fastened by its
underside and carries a part on its top declares its holes twice: the two faces'
holes are then two holes in this version, so a screw that would pass through
the rail and the parts on both sides of it, one screw through three parts, is
not refused there. An interface that lists holes on the face a part is glued by, its `dir`
along that of the connector the part is glued by, says how the part could be
held there, so a program that glues the part lists it as undecided, without a
warning (`assembly.parts_held`): for want of an `on`, or, where other parts are
fastened onto those holes, naming them; holes on another face do not, nor does
a grid, since a part is not fastened by one.
The result `--json` writes and `compile.json` give
each part's interfaces, in the part's own frame ([the command line](cli.md)).

#### Grids

A grid's holes stand at the points of a lattice: one of `diameter` at every
`pos + u * up + v * (dir x up)` for each offset `u` and each offset `v`, but
the points `except` names. The top of a goBILDA channel is an 8 mm grid with
no hole at the points beside its bores:

```yaml
interfaces:
  middle_top:
    pos: [0, 0, 0.024]
    dir: [0, 0, 1]
    up: [1, 0, 0]
    fastener_diameter: 0.004
    threaded: false
    grid:
      u: [-0.016, -0.008, 0.008, 0.016]          # offsets along up, listed
      v: {from: -0.124, to: 0.124, step: 0.008}  # offsets along dir x up, in whole steps
      diameter: 0.004
      except: [[-0.008, -0.108], [0.008, -0.108], [-0.008, -0.084], [0.008, -0.084]]
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `u`, `v` | yes | The offsets along the pattern's two axes: a list of at least one, each greater than the one before, or `{from, to, step}`, from `from` up to `to` in whole steps of `step` (positive) |
| `diameter` | yes | The diameter of every hole of the grid, less than its least spacing |
| `except` | no | The points that hold no hole, each `[u, v]`: a point of the grid, named once. At least one point holds a hole |

The u axis is `up` made square to `dir`, as a connector's frame is built, so
every point lies on the face. A hole of the grid is named by its point, its
site. A feature wider one way at a site, such as goBILDA's slots, is declared
by its narrowest width there, as a round hole. A grid of more than 200,000
points is refused, as a file of more values is.

### Storage regions

A chassis, a mount or an attachment may keep other parts in regions of its own:
`storage` maps a name, an identifier that is not the name of one of the part's
connectors or interfaces, to a region. A compartment closed by walls and by a
cover below, which the pack it keeps sits on:

```yaml
storage:
  compartment:
    seat: pack_seat                  # the connector a kept part is seated on
    box: {size: [0.08, 0.05, 0.02], origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0.0125]}
    sides: {-x: wall, +x: wall, -y: wall, +y: wall, -z: cover, +z: wall}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seat` | yes | A connector of the part, inside the box, that states an `up` and no `well`. A part placed on it is stored in the region, turned by the seat's `up` and its own connector's |
| `box` | yes | `size` (three positive numbers) and `origin_xyz`: a box square to the part frame, within its declared collision bound (a box, a hull, or a compound's outer bound), allowing 1 µm. Ordinary storage cannot hold the whole collision shape, because it removes that material. A capture region removes no material and may bound the whole holder. A part without a declared shape collides by its mesh, which the compiler does not open, and its box is not checked against it |
| `sides` | yes | What closes each side of the box, all six stated: `-x`, `+x`, `-y`, `+y`, `-z` and `+z`, each `wall` (the part's own material), `cover`, `strap`, `end_stop` (an element the part comes with) or `open` (nothing does), or `friction` (retention depends on an unverified friction/preload relationship) |
| `capture` | no | `true` makes the region capture a named feature instead of containing the entire payload; see [Partial capture](#partial-capture). The default is whole-part storage |

A part is stored in a region when it is placed on the region's seat: by a glue
onto the seat, as a part is glued onto any connector, or with `on` naming the
part and `at` the region, which carries it with its host ([The
robot](../guide/basics/robot.md#parts-stored-in-a-region)). The seat is one
connector, so it takes one part, and no two regions of a part share one. The
seat states its `up`, since the box is square to the part: a part seated there
lies as the two `up`s say, and a stored part whose connector states none, being
the same however turned, lies as a glue would put it. A
stored part is held where every side is closed and its declared shape lies
within the box, within 2 mm; otherwise `assembly.parts_held` lists it as
undecided, naming each side its part states `open` as `storage.<region>.sides.<side>`.
No rule tells `wall`, `cover`, `strap` and `end_stop` apart in this version:
the rules treat both `open` and `friction` as unknown, and the words say what retains a part
where a person reads it. The box is a void in the part's declared shape for the
clearance rules, as a well is: a part lies inside the shape as far as the box
and no further, and one that crosses the shape outside the box is judged by
the depth it reaches into the shape beyond the box's faces. `parts[]` in the
result `--json` writes, and in `compile.json`, gives each part's regions in its
own frame ([the command line](cli.md)).

### Partial capture

A dock may hold an arm's base while its links extend beyond it. The payload
names that actual local feature and its mating connector:

```yaml
capture_features:
  base:
    connector: mount
    box: {size: [0.110, 0.090, 0.013], origin_xyz: [-0.0125, 0, 0.0065]}
```

The holder declares a `storage` region with `capture: true`, a seat, a box
bounding the retained feature and all six retaining sides. The program selects
it with `on`, `at` and the required `by` feature name. The selected feature's
connector, not the payload's default connector, mates to the seat. It must state
an `up` because the feature box has a specific orientation. The feature
must fit within 1 micrometre; the ordinary 2 mm coarse-shape allowance does not
establish a capture fit. Changing `turn_rad` changes the fit too. A missing
feature name is rejected; glue alone cannot choose one and leaves holding unknown.

Every positively closed side and a fitting feature establish `means: captured`.
An `open` or `friction` side, a shared seat, or an unheld parent Mount keeps the
hold unknown. This checks the declared geometric restraint; it does not compute
load capacity, tightening force, friction, deformation, pin wear or impact strength.
A circular pin or tube grip needs its actual retaining facts; a bounding box alone
does not establish radial engagement or preload.

A capture region is **not a collision void**. Its box removes no material from
the holder, and the complete payload and its links remain collision-checked.
Describe a fork or a holder's actual material with compound boxes when needed;
ordinary whole-part storage retains its existing void semantics. The compiler
does not infer that a side is closed from the presence of a CAD mesh.

### Mounts

An entry of category `mount` is a part whose only job is to hold other parts
of the robot: a plate, a bracket, an adapter, a standoff, a riser, a clamp, a
holder. A program places it as a `Mount` ([The
robot](../guide/basics/robot.md#mounts)). It states the holes it is fastened
by and holds other parts by under `interfaces`, and the regions it keeps them
in under `storage`. It may state neither: a clamp that grips a tube holds by
friction, with no hole or region to state, and a plate whose holes are not yet
measured states none. A set used together, such as four standoffs under one
board, is one part, stating every hole of the set. A mount has no electrical
role, so it states no `power_input`, `power_outputs` or `ports`, and it moves
no body of its own, so it states no `links`. A part that holds others and has
a job of its own besides, such as a pan-tilt head that turns what it holds on
its servos, is an attachment.

### Links

A chassis, an attachment or a leg may move bodies of its own below its frame:
a legged robot's legs, a pan-tilt mount's head, a leg's thigh and shin. `links`
maps each
link's name, an identifier, to what it states, each link after the one it
hangs from:

```yaml
links:
  head:
    parent: null                     # the part frame, or a link declared above this one
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, 0.02], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 0, 1], range: [-1.57, 1.57]}
    inertial:
      mass: 0.04
      origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0.015]
      inertia: {ixx: 1.1e-05, ixy: 0, ixz: 0, iyy: 1.1e-05, iyz: 0, izz: 1.0e-05}
      source: estimated
      basis: a 40 g servo of 30 by 50 by 30 mm
    visual: {file: assets/head.glb, xyz: [0, 0, 0], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
    collision:                       # the shapes it collides by; absent when it touches nothing
      - {type: box, size: [0.03, 0.05, 0.03], origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0.015], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
    servo: {kp: 4.0, damping: 0.05, armature: 0.0002, frictionloss: 0.01, effort: 0.6, hold: 0.5}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `parent` | yes | `null` for the part frame, or the name of a link declared above this one |
| `joint` | yes | `type`, `xyz`, `rpy`: the link's frame is its parent's, moved to `xyz` and turned by the fixed-axis roll, pitch and yaw `rpy`. A `revolute` joint then turns it about `axis`, a unit vector in the link's own frame, within `range: [lowest, highest]`, in radians, the lowest below the highest. A `prismatic` joint translates along its local unit axis, with range and position in metres. A `continuous` joint rotates in radians about its unit axis and declares no range. A `fixed` joint states no axis, range, position or mimic |
| `inertial` | required for base-scoped parts; absent for assembly scope | As a part's, in the link's frame. A link cannot declare assembly scope |
| `visual` | yes | As a part's, in the link's frame |
| `collision` | no | A list of at least one shape, as an object's, in the link's frame, or a `capsule`, a cylinder with half a sphere on each end: its diameter in `x` and in `z` the distance between the centres of its two ends. Without it the link collides with nothing |
| `servo` | optional on an independent moving joint; forbidden on fixed or mimic joints | The position servo that turns the joint, as a simulator holds it: `kp` (N m/rad, positive), how stiffly it pulls toward the angle it is told; optional `kv` (N m s/rad, nonnegative), its actuator velocity feedback; `damping` (N m s/rad), `armature`, the turning inertia of its motor behind its gearbox (kg m²), and `frictionloss` (N m), none negative; `effort` (N m, positive), the most torque it gives; `hold`, within the joint's range, the angle it holds when nothing commands it (rad); and `basis`, when given, where the values come from. `kv` is bounded by the actuator's effort together with position feedback; passive joint `damping` is separate. Without `kv`, no velocity feedback parameter is emitted. Nothing stands in for a value the library does not state |

Each independent moving joint requires an explicit `joint.position` or a complete `servo`.
When position is omitted, legacy `servo.hold` supplies it; when both are present they must
agree. No missing position becomes zero. Position and range use radians for revolute joints
and metres for prismatic joints. Continuous positions use radians without a mechanical range;
they are finite but never wrapped or clamped. Continuous joints reject a declared range.

`joint.mimic: {link: source_link, multiplier: 1, offset: 0}` gives the follower position as
`multiplier * source_position + offset`. All three fields are explicit. The source must be
another moving link; it can be declared later. Cycles are rejected. A follower states no
independent position or servo, and its derived position must be in its own range. The offset
uses the follower's unit; multiplier uses follower-unit/source-unit, including m/rad or rad/m
for a rotary-to-linear coupling. Continuous sources and followers use radians as revolute joints do. This checks the stated configuration, not every possible
source-joint excursion or a nonlinear linkage.

By default, the part's own `inertial.scope` is `base`: its mass is the base alone, and every
link requires a separate inertial. Do not put a product's entire mass into that base and add
its link masses again. When only an aggregate product mass, centre of mass and tensor are
known, `scope: assembly` retains them at the declared static configuration and counts them
exactly once. Assembly scope requires links and forbids their inertial blocks; it does not
invent a distribution among bodies. Geometry can be split into source-backed link visuals
without changing aggregate mass or claiming dynamic parameters are known.

The compiler places links at their explicit or derived static positions for inspection,
footprint and inter-part clearance. A sphere and a capsule are
judged for clearance as they are, by the distance from the sphere's centre or
from the segment between the capsule's two centres less the radius; only to
tell whether a well lets one in is it taken as the solid of flat faces drawn
around it, whose corners stand no more than 1.74 % of its radius past it, so that a
well never lets in more than it holds. A part's own links are not judged
against each other or against its base, which they meet at their joints. A well
on a connector lets things only into the part's own declared shape, never into a
link's: a clearance finding names the shape it is of, and for a link advises a
tighter shape, or, when its joint or one it hangs from turns, that joint's servo
holding it elsewhere. The `mjcf` target writes a part's links, each a body on
a hinge its servo turns or fixed to the link above it
([the output reference](output.md#the-mjcf-target));
`ros-gz-nav2` and `ros-mujoco-nav2` do not write them yet, and refuse such a
part (`target.unsupported`).

### Feet and gait

A chassis used as `Legged` walks on legs: its own links, or legs that are
parts of their own placed on it ([Legs as parts](#legs-as-parts)). Its profiles
list `Legged`, with at least one mount, such as a deck others mount on; it states
what its walking controller takes, and, when its legs are its own, its `links`
and the shapes on them it stands on:

```yaml
profiles:
  Legged: {mounts: {deck: deck}}
feet:                                # the shapes on its links that stand on the floor
  front_left: {link: FL_knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
  front_right: {link: FR_knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
gait: {ahead: [-0.5, 1.0], aside: [-0.4, 0.4], turn: [-1.0, 1.0]}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feet` | a leg's, and a `Legged` chassis's whose legs are its own, required; no other part's | Each foot by a name, an identifier: the `link` it is on, the `shape` it is among that link's `collision`, counting from 0, a sphere, a capsule or a box, and the `friction` it grips the floor with (positive). Two feet name two shapes |
| `gait` | a `Legged` chassis's, required; no other part's | What its walking controller takes, in the chassis frame: `ahead` and `aside`, its speeds ahead and to its left (m/s), and `turn`, its turn to the left (rad/s), each `[lowest, highest]` with standing still, 0, among them |

The robot stands where the servos hold its legs, each `hold`: the compiler finds
each foot's points lowest down there, below a sphere's centre, below a capsule's
lower end or both ends of one lying flat, a box's lowest corners, each point
within 2 mm of the foot's lowest standing with it, as the feet stand within 2 mm
of one plane; the ground is where they stand. `assembly.feet_touch_the_ground`
asks that every foot stand on the ground with the others, and points at the foot
and at the servos that hold it; `assembly.wheels_touch_one_plane` asks the same of
a wheel or a caster placed under the chassis; and `assembly.links_clear_the_ground`
that no other shape of the links reach below the ground, which finds a foot named
by the wrong shape. The statics rule takes the feet as the robot's supports, and
cannot judge them while one stands off the ground.

The gait says which way and how fast the base goes. A `Spin` needs a turn that
way and a `Strafe` a speed aside to that side, an `Advance` and a `Navigate` a
speed ahead and a `BackUp` one back, and a `speed_mps` the task states may be no
more than the gait's that way (`kinematics.spin_supported`,
`kinematics.strafe_supported` and `kinematics.walk_supported`). A `Navigate`
needs a turn either way, as a navigation planner turns a robot either way to follow its path.
An `Advance`, a `BackUp` or a `Strafe` without a speed is judged by its way
alone: the speed it goes at is the target's.

The feet and the gait are the `Legged` type's, and a leg's feet are its own. A
part whose profiles list another type too stands, used as that type, on that
type's wheels or tracks, its feet being shapes of its links like the rest. A
`Legged` chassis has no wheel or track mounts. The two ROS targets refuse a legged
base for its links, its part's or its legs'; the `mjcf` target writes one that
walks by the walking controller its part states, or by a [walker](#walkers), and
one that walks by neither standing, the model a walker for it is trained on.

#### Legs as parts

A leg may be a part of its own, of category `leg`, used as a `Leg`: a leg made
or sold apart from the body it walks under, placed by glue on a `Legged` chassis
that has no legs of its own. Such a chassis is a body: it states its `gait`, and
no `feet`, and walks by the gait its controller states or by a
[walker](#walkers) trained for it on its legs; links of its own, a head or arms,
are no legs, and a gait holds them where their servos hold them. Each leg states
its `links`, on hinges its servos turn from its frame down, and the `feet` on
them, as a chassis's own legs do, and neither a `gait` nor a `controller`: the
chassis's controller, or its walker, walks all its legs together.

```yaml
# parts/hip_leg/component.yaml, in part
category: leg
connectors:
  mount: {pos: [0, 0, 0], dir: [0, 0, 1], up: [1, 0, 0]}   # where it meets the body
profiles:
  Leg: {mounts: {default: mount}}
links:                               # a thigh on a hip and a shin on a knee, both pitching
  hip:
    parent: null
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, 0], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 1, 0], range: [-1.5, 1.5]}
    # its inertial, visual, collision and servo, as under Links
  knee:
    parent: hip
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, -0.15], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 1, 0], range: [-2.6, 0]}
    # the same; its second collision shape is a ball at the shin's end
feet:                                # the ball the leg stands on
  foot: {link: knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
```

```robotdsl
Robot quad {
    Legged body(ref = "quad_body")
    Leg front_left(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg front_right(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg rear_left(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (-0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg rear_right(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (-0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
}
```

The robot stands on the feet of all its legs, each foot named by its leg in a
finding, and every rule above takes them as it takes a chassis's own.
`assembly.legs_on_a_legged_chassis` asks that every leg be placed on a `Legged`
chassis with no legs of its own, hanging from no connector of it that steers, and
that such a chassis carry legs: a leg on a base that rolls would hang from it, a
chassis with legs of its own walks on them alone, as its walking controller was
made for them, and a leg on a mount that steers, or on a part on that mount, would
turn about a kingpin no servo turns. A leg on a part fixed to the chassis, a
spacer, hangs as fixed as one on the chassis. A policy in a part's controller
was trained on the legs it walks, the part's own, so a chassis with no feet of
its own walks by a gait, or by a walker trained for it on its legs; a policy in
its own controller is refused.

### Walking controller

A `Legged` chassis may state the walking controller its legs walk by: a
policy, an ONNX file in the part's directory, that a page or a simulator calls
every so often with what it observes, and whose action sets the servos' targets;
or a gait, which needs no training ([below](#a-gait)), the one a chassis whose
legs are parts placed on it walks by. Without one the part loads and the
analysis and the rules judge it as they judge any; the `mjcf` target writes a
legged base only by its controller, or by a [walker](#walkers) trained for it.

```yaml
controller:
  policy: assets/policy.onnx     # an ONNX file in the part directory
  period: 0.02                   # s between two calls
  imu: {link: null, xyz: [-0.016, -0.067, -0.006], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
  observation: [linear_velocity, angular_velocity, gravity, joint_angles,
                joint_velocities, last_action, command]
  action_scale: 0.5              # a servo's target: its hold plus this times the action
  simulator: {timestep: 0.004, integrator: Euler, iterations: 1, ls_iterations: 5,
              eulerdamp: false}
  basis: MuJoCo Playground's go1_policy.onnx (Apache-2.0)
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `policy` | yes | The policy, an ONNX file inside the part directory. The compiler copies it as it is and reads nothing of it |
| `period` | yes | The time between two calls (s), a whole number of the simulator's steps |
| `imu` | yes | Where the IMU is whose readings the policy observes: the `link` it is on, null for the part's frame, and its place `xyz` and turn `rpy` there |
| `observation` | yes | What the policy observes, each term once, in its order: `linear_velocity`, the IMU's linear velocity in its own frame; `angular_velocity`, its angular velocity; `gravity`, straight down, (0, 0, -1), in its frame, the transpose of its turn applied to it; `command`, ahead, to the left and turning left; `joint_angles`, each servo's angle from its `hold`, in the order of the part's links; `joint_velocities`, their speeds; `last_action`, the action it gave last; and `phase`, the gait's phase, the cosine of each foot's and then their sines |
| `hidden` | no | Links whose servos the policy reads as still: their angle and their speed read 0 |
| `action_scale` | yes | Each servo's target is its `hold` plus this times the action's term for it (positive) |
| `phase` | when `observation` lists `phase`, and only then | The gait's `frequency` (Hz) and each phase's offset, `offsets` (rad), at least one; with both `still_below` (positive) and `still_at`, each phase reads `still_at` while the command's length is under `still_below`, and goes on turning meanwhile |
| `simulator` | yes | The simulator the policy was trained in, as MuJoCo's `<option>` states it: `timestep` (s), `integrator` (`Euler`, `implicit` or `implicitfast`: not `RK4`, since the model is stepped in two halves, `mj_step1`, the controls, then `mj_step2`, which integrates by Euler under `RK4`), the solver's `iterations` and `ls_iterations` (whole, from 1 to 2147483647, the most MuJoCo reads), and `eulerdamp`, whether Euler's integrator damps the joints implicitly |
| `basis` | yes | Where the policy comes from |

The policy moves the chassis's servos, in the order of its links; the servos of
the parts mounted on it hold where they hold.

#### A gait

The walking controller may instead be a gait, which needs no training: a page or
a simulator works it out from the robot's own model as the robot walks. The legs,
taken in turn about the chassis's middle, step every other one half a period
apart. The feet on the floor carry the body level at its standing height and at
the speed it is told, and each foot in the air lands where that speed needs it.
The command it follows moves toward the one it is told by at most 1 m/s and
2 rad/s each second, so that told to stop at once from a run it slows over a
moment; it goes on stepping until the robot has settled, moving and turning
hardly at all at a period's workings of the gait in a row, and stops with
every foot down. [The output contract](output.md#the-mjcf-target) says how.

```yaml
controller:
  gait: {period: 0.4, duty: 0.55, step_height: 0.07}
  basis: a gait from the part's own model, with no training
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gait.period` | yes | The time a foot takes to step and stand again (s, positive) |
| `gait.duty` | yes | The part of the period each foot is on the floor: more than 0.5 and less than 1. Every foot is on the floor together for (duty - 0.5) times the period, twice a period, and the gait stops only then, once the robot has settled: at least 8 ms, two of the 4 ms the gait is worked out every. Each foot is in the air for (1 - duty) times the period, at least 40 ms, ten of them, to follow its arc |
| `gait.step_height` | yes | How high a foot is lifted (m, positive) |
| `basis` | yes | Where the gait's numbers come from |

A gait lifts every other leg, so the robot stands on an even number of feet,
four or more: a robot on two feet is balanced otherwise, which this version does
not do. Each foot steps by at least two servos between it and its part's frame,
one to lift it and one to swing it, and by servos of its own: a servo above two
feet, such as a spine's or a waist's, is not stepped by a gait in this version.
The loader asks this of a chassis's own legs, and
`kinematics.gait_walks_the_feet` of the robot's, the legs placed on it too. A leg
whose servos only pitch steps fore and aft alone, so the robot turns by the
strides of its sides, slowly; its `gait` states the turn it reaches. A gait
balances the model as it is, with the parts mounted on the chassis, and moves the
servos of the feet's legs; every other servo holds where it holds.

### Walkers

A robot assembled from a `Legged` body and legs that are parts of their own
walks by the gait its body states, which needs no training, or by a walker: a
policy trained for exactly that robot, which the library registers beside its
parts. A program whose `Legged` body and legs are a walker's walks by the
walker, whatever its body states, and takes the command the walker takes; the
`mjcf` target writes the walker's policy as the robot's drive. Its legs are the
walker's when each is the same part as one of the walker's, placed within a
millimetre of where the analysis places that one by its glue and turned within a
milliradian of how it turns it, each leg one of the walker's and each of the
walker's one leg, in whatever order the program declares them. Parts a program
mounts besides are carried, a load the policy was not trained with. Two walkers
of a library for the same robot are refused (`assembly.one_walker`): which one
the robot walks by is not the program's to say.

```yaml
# walkers/quad_walker/walker.yaml
schema_version: 1
id: quad_walker
description: the body on its four legs, walking by a policy trained for it
assembly:
  body: quad_body                  # a Legged chassis part without legs of its own
  limbs:                           # each leg on it, by a name of the walker's own
    fl: {part: hip_leg, glue: [0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    fr: {part: hip_leg, glue: [0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    rl: {part: hip_leg, glue: [-0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    rr: {part: hip_leg, glue: [-0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
gait: {ahead: [-0.3, 0.6], aside: [-0.2, 0.2], turn: [-0.8, 0.8]}
controller:
  policy: assets/policy.onnx
  joints: [fl/hip, fl/knee, fr/hip, fr/knee, rl/hip, rl/knee, rr/hip, rr/knee]
  period: 0.02
  imu: {link: null, xyz: [0, 0, 0.02], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
  observation: [linear_velocity, angular_velocity, gravity, command, joint_angles,
                joint_velocities, last_action]
  action_scale: 0.25
  simulator: {timestep: 0.004, integrator: Euler, iterations: 1, ls_iterations: 5,
              eulerdamp: false}
  basis: trained on the body on its four legs, in MuJoCo
provenance: {name: The body on its four legs, manufacturer: null, source_url: null, license: null}
```

| --- | --- | --- |
| `assembly.body` | yes | The body the walker was trained with: a chassis part of the library with a `Legged` profile and no legs of its own |
| `assembly.limbs` | yes | Each leg placed on the body, by a name of the walker's own, any but `body`: its `part`, a leg of the library, and its `glue`, x, y and z, the unit normal nx, ny and nz and, when the program states one, the roll about it, as a program places it |
| `gait` | yes | The command the policy takes, its ranges as a `Legged` chassis states them |
| `controller` | yes | The policy, as a part's [walking controller](#walking-controller) states it, and `joints`: every servo of the body and its legs, each once, as `owner/link`, the owner `body` or a limb's name, in the order the policy reads and moves them. `hidden` names servos as `joints` does, and the IMU's `link` is one of the body's links, or null for its frame |

A walker that does not state a robot of the library's parts, whose file gives a
key twice, whose policy does not move every servo of it or has none to move, or
that places two legs of one part by glues within twice that millimetre and
milliradian of each other, where a leg placed between them would be either, is a
diagnostic, and the robot does not walk by it; the parts still load.

### Objects

An entry of category `object` is a thing a world places, a table, a shelf, a
ramp, and not a part of a robot. A `.world` entity names it by `ref`. It
states what is shown of it and what of it collides:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: ramp_10deg                       # equals the directory name
category: object
description: A ramp 0.8 m wide that rises 10 degrees along +x over one metre, from the floor at its frame.

visual:                              # the mesh that is shown
  file: assets/model.glb
  xyz: [0, 0, 0]
  rpy: [0, 0, 0]

collision:                           # the shapes it collides by; absent when it is only shown
  - type: box                        # box | sphere | cylinder
    size: [1.01543, 0.8, 0.05]       # a slab, tilted so that its top face is the ramp's surface
    origin_xyz: [0.50434, 0, 0.06354]
    rpy: [0, -0.174533, 0]

provenance:
  name: null
  manufacturer: null
  source_url: null
  license: null
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version`, `id`, `category`, `description` | yes | As for a part; `category` is `object` |
| `visual` | yes | As for a part: the mesh a simulator shows, with where it sits in the object's frame |
| `collision` | no | A list of at least one shape. Each states `type` (`box`, `sphere` or `cylinder`), `size` (three positive numbers: a box's sides; a sphere's diameter and a cylinder's in `x`, a cylinder's height in `z`, as a world entity's `size` reads), `origin_xyz` and `rpy`, its place and its fixed-axis roll, pitch and yaw in the object's frame. The targets collide the object by these shapes, the navigation map is drawn from them and a run is judged against them, each shape projected onto the ground where the entity stands. Without `collision` the object is only shown, and no entity that collides can be made of it |
| `provenance` | no | As for a part, without a price: an object is not bought. Of an object whose mesh is a model someone else published, `name` is the model, `manufacturer` its author, `source_url` where it lies and `license` the licence it is passed on under |

An object collides by shapes and never by its mesh. The compiler opens no
mesh, so it could neither draw one onto the map nor judge a run against it,
and the two simulators would not agree on it: MuJoCo collides a mesh by its
convex hull, which fills the space under a table, and reads no glTF.

Both simulators take a mesh's coordinates as they are, in metres with z up,
after the transforms of the file's nodes; neither turns a glTF from its y-up
convention. Gazebo decodes the mesh. MuJoCo decodes no glTF, so the
`ros-mujoco-nav2` target's node reads it: a `.glb`, or a `.gltf` with its
buffers beside it or written into it, as every triangle of the file's default
scene in its material's base colour (`baseColorFactor`) with the picture laid
on it (`baseColorTexture`), without the material's other maps, the light it
states it gives off (`emissiveFactor`), normals or vertex colours. It does not read a mesh that requires an extension (a
compressed or quantized mesh), a sparse accessor, anything drawn as points,
lines, strips or fans, a picture that is not a PNG, which is all MuJoCo
decodes, or one moved or scaled where it is laid (`KHR_texture_transform`):
the node stops as it starts and says which stands in the way. Of an object whose mesh is not glTF that target shows the
shapes the object collides by, and it refuses one that only shows
(`target.unsupported`), of which nothing would be in the scene.

An object states none of `inertial`, `connectors`, `profiles`, `wheel`,
`track`, `range`, `motor`, `battery`, `driver`, `power_input`, `power_outputs`,
`ports`, `interfaces`, `storage` and `contacts`; each is `library.unsupported` on it. A world holds an object
where the program places it, so it states no mass; nothing mates onto it, so
it states no connectors; and whether the robot may touch it is the entity
type's to say in the world that places it, so it states no profiles.

### Environments

An entry of category `environment` is a place a `.world` scenario takes whole
by `ref`: a room, a hall with its shelves. It has no mesh and no shape of its
own; it states its floor and the entities that stand in it.

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: room_6x4                         # equals the directory name; never `empty`
category: environment
description: A storeroom 6 m by 4 m with walls 0.5 m high, a work table in a corner and a mark on the floor where a robot docks.

ground_plane: true                   # whether it brings its floor

entities:                            # name -> what a .world entity states
  wall_north: {entity: Obstacle, type: box, size: [6.2, 0.1, 0.5], pos: [2, 2.05, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
  table: {entity: Obstacle, ref: work_table, pos: [4.5, 1.1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
  dock: {entity: Marker, ref: floor_disc, pos: [4.0, -1.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version`, `id`, `category`, `description` | yes | As for a part; `category` is `environment`. The id may not be `empty`, which a scenario writes for no environment |
| `ground_plane` | yes | `true` or `false`: whether the environment brings its floor, which is the world's one ground plane. No scenario of a world that takes such an environment may add `ground_plane = true`; two environments that each bring a floor share the one |
| `entities` | yes | A mapping, which may be empty, from an entity's name (an identifier) to its fields, below |
| `provenance` | no | As for a part |

An entity's fields are the [parameters of a `.world` entity](vocabulary.md#entity-types),
by their names and in their forms, so that the lines of a scenario move into a
library unchanged in meaning:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `entity` | yes | The entity type: `Obstacle`, `SupportSurface` or `Marker`. The vocabulary's, so it is resolved when a program takes the environment |
| `type` | one of `type` and `ref` | A primitive: `box`, `sphere` or `cylinder` |
| `size` | with `type`; not with `ref` | `[x, y, z]`, positive, as a `.world` entity's |
| `ref` | one of `type` and `ref` | The id of a library [object](#objects). It may be another library's that the program is compiled with, so it is resolved when a program takes the environment |
| `pos` | yes | `[x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw]` in the world's frame; the quaternion of unit length |
| `collision` | no | `true` or `false`; without it the entity type decides, as in a `.world` file |

An environment's entities are static, like every entity, and state no
`is_static`. A scenario takes them where they stand: it gives the environment
no pose. Once taken they are the scenario's own entities, in the world's one
namespace beside the program's.

### Ports and buses

A part that is commanded or read, or that commands and reads others, states
its ports, one for each socket, by the name its board prints. Three parts'
blocks, each from its own `component.yaml`:

```yaml
ports:                                     # a computer's
  usb3_0: {kind: usb, role: host}          # one port for each socket
  usb3_1: {kind: usb, role: host}
  i2c1: {kind: i2c, role: controller}
  uart0: {kind: uart}
  eth: {kind: ethernet}
ports:                                     # the MinIMU-9 v6's: as sold, and with its SA0 pin low
  i2c: {kind: i2c, role: target, address: [0x6b, 0x1e], addresses: [[0x6a, 0x1c]]}
ports:                                     # a motor controller commanded over I²C
  i2c: {kind: i2c, role: target, address: 0x10, addresses: any}   # 16 as sold, any other by a command
```

Two ports join when they are of one kind, in complementary roles where the
kind has two: a USB device a USB host, an I²C target an I²C controller, a
UART a UART, an Ethernet port an Ethernet port, and a port of kind `bus` one on
the same bus. A USB port, a UART, an Ethernet port and an I²C target each join
one other port, so a hub is an ordinary part with a device port and host
ports; an I²C controller and a bus join any number. Which of a program's links
join which ports, and what that leaves undecided, the [link
rules](../guide/advanced/validation.md#is-every-motor-commanded-and-every-link-joined) say.

An I²C target states the address it answers at as sold, `address`: one, or
the list of those a board of several chips answers at together. `addresses`
states what else it may be set to, each choice of the shape of `address`, or
`any`, any one address, for a target of one address that a command sets. A
target sold with no address of its own states `addresses` alone, and its program
names the one it is set to. An address is written as its maker prints it,
`0x6b`, quoted or not, and is one of 0x08 to 0x77, those the I²C specification
leaves to targets. A number without `0x` is refused: `i2cdetect` prints
addresses in hexadecimal without it and datasheets write `68h`, so `68` may
mean either. A choice is not the address as sold and is given once. A target
whose part states no address may answer at any, and the rules say what that
leaves undecided.

A bus name is the library's own: the compiler only compares it, a motor's
`bus` with the `buses` of the driver that commands it, and a port's `bus` with
another's. Name the wire and the protocol together (`dynamixel_ttl`,
`dynamixel_rs485`), since two makers' servos on the same wire do not answer
each other's boards. A motor driver states the buses it speaks once, in its
`driver` block, and a link meets each as a port named by its bus, so its
`ports` state no `bus` port and name none of its ports as one of its buses.
Neither block is defaulted: a part that states no ports has not said that it
has none.

### Power inputs and outputs

A part a program feeds states what it takes for its power, and a part that feeds others
states what it feeds them from. A motor states the supply it accepts in its `motor` block and a
motor driver in its `driver` block; a sensor, attachment, chassis or leg states its known
external input in `power_input`.
Three parts' blocks, each from its own `component.yaml`:

```yaml
power_input: {voltage_min_v: 4.5, voltage_max_v: 5.5}   # the supply it accepts: the LD06's
power_input: {voltage_nominal_v: 5}                      # the one voltage it is sold for
power_input: none                                        # it takes no power: a switch its host reads
```

The voltage a part is sold for decides nothing alone: whether it takes the supply around that
voltage is its maker's to state, as Raspberry Pi states "5V/5A" for the Pi 5 and no range. A
part fed a supply that states no range it accepts is warned of, and the warning shows where the
supply lies against the voltage it is sold for. A sensor takes power unless its part states
`power_input: none`; an attachment, chassis or leg is judged as an external load when its part
states a power input or outputs, or when its program names its `power`. An undeclared
attachment is otherwise carried, as an arm or a tray is. No external supply, internal
battery, controller or electrical load is inferred from a chassis's or leg's shape, links
or ports. A data-only chassis may state ports while its internal power topology remains
unmodeled. `power_input: none` means explicitly no power, and is not a substitute for
unknown internal topology; an empty `power_input: {}` is invalid.

```yaml
power_outputs:                       # what the part feeds others from, each by its name
  out: {voltage_nominal_v: 5, voltage_min_v: 4.8, voltage_max_v: 5.2}   # a regulator's 5 V within 4 %
  5v: {passes_input: true}           # what the part is fed, passed on: a computer's 5 V pins
```

An output states the voltage it is sold by and, when its maker states them, the least and the
most it delivers, its tolerance included. One that states only its nominal leaves the voltage
rules undecided, as a pack that states only its nominal does. An output that passes on what its
part is fed states no voltage of its own: a computer's 5 V pins give what its USB-C input is
given. A sensor, attachment, chassis, leg, motor driver and motor with a `bus`, which passes its supply
down its chain, may state outputs; a battery delivers by its `battery` block, and a motor
without a bus gives nothing on. A motor driver's `output_voltage_v` is not an output: it is the
voltage its channels feed its motors. Neither block is defaulted. A part that states no
outputs has not said that it has none, so a program may name it as a supply, and the rules say
what that leaves undecided ([What the compiler checks](../guide/advanced/validation.md#does-every-part-get-its-power)).

What a source delivers, and what a part draws, are stated where their makers state them, and
the current rules add up the draws behind each source. For a sensor whose source gives only
a typical current, retain its voltage range and leave the current unknown:

```yaml
power_input: {voltage_min_v: 4.5, voltage_max_v: 5.5}  # typical current is not a bound
```

```yaml
# Pololu D36V50F5: current and efficiency are specified as typical, not bounds.
power_input: {voltage_min_v: 5.5, voltage_max_v: 50}
power_outputs:
  out: {voltage_nominal_v: 5, voltage_min_v: 4.8, voltage_max_v: 5.2}
```

A battery and an output state the current they deliver continuously, `continuous_current_a`,
and beside it what they deliver for a moment, `peak_current_a`; a motor driver states what its
channels deliver together, `continuous_current_total_a` and `peak_current_total_a`, where its
maker rates them below what they deliver each. A peak is stated with the continuous current,
which the continuous rule judges a source by. An output at a voltage of its own, and a driver
that regulates what it feeds its motors, state their `efficiency`, the fraction of the power
they take that they deliver. Where a maker gives what a source delivers, or an efficiency, as
a guaranteed range, the part states the least of it over its accepted conditions. A typical
capacity or efficiency curve is not a guaranteed lower bound; omit those fields when only
typical values are available.

A part states what it draws itself in its `power_input`: a sensor working, a regulator board
its quiescent current, a motor driver beside what its motors draw. The current rules read it as
the most the part draws, so state only a source-qualified maximum. Pololu's typical 2–4 mA
quiescent range is not such a bound. A typical or average current is not an upper bound: omit it even if a comment
could identify its qualification. A motor states none: it draws its stall current as it starts.
A figure a maker does not state stays out: the rules name the missing field.

`power_input.startup_current_a` states the part's own maximum power-on current in amperes,
when the source explicitly bounds it. It is optional and nonnegative, including zero for a
board that draws nothing itself. It is independent of `continuous_current_a`: neither value
is inferred from the other, and neither is required to be larger. A driver may state its own
electronics' startup current here, separately from the motors on its channels. Do not enter a
recommended supply rating, average, typical value or minimum as a consumer-current bound.

The simultaneous power-on rule uses this field for nonmotors and the existing stall bounds
for motors, through the same converter voltage and efficiency bounds. It compares against a
source's peak current, falling back to continuous capacity. Missing startup bounds leave the
answer unknown. These are static capacity bounds; peak duration, transient waveform, current
limiting and power sequencing are not modeled. A pass of the separate motor-stall rule assumes
other loads are already running and does not establish cold-start capacity.

### Profiles

A profile is one component type the part can be used as, named exactly as the
vocabulary names the type, and maps the logical mount names of that type to
the part's connectors. The `Mecanum_four_wheel` profile of a frame maps
`front_left_wheel`, ..., and `middle_top`; a wheel's or a sensor's profile
maps `default`, the connector the part mates by, and so do a battery's and a
motor driver's; a track's maps `default`, the hub that drives it, whose
connector carries no joint, since the unit does not turn about its hub; a motor's maps `default`, the
face it seats on a chassis' drive mount by, and `shaft`, the end of its output
shaft, where a wheel mates. The shaft connector carries no joint: the wheel's
connector carries the `continuous` joint, so the joint is between motor and
wheel. Two logical mounts may not share a connector. Which types exist and
which mounts each needs is vocabulary, decided by the semantic phase, not by
this format.

A profile maps mounts and nothing else. Which mounts of a chassis type steer
is vocabulary; which of them are driven is what the program places, a motor on
the mount or on a seat whose driveline turns it, within what the type allows.

## Diagnostics

Every problem is a diagnostic in the `library_load` phase that points into
the file. A problem with `library.yaml` itself blocks: nothing can be loaded.
A part with any problem in its declaration is left out of the loaded library,
so later phases never see a half-checked record, and the diagnostic is a
warning that does not block a program which never names the part; a program
that names such a part gets a name-resolution error that repeats why the part
could not be loaded. A shared catalog with a few incomplete declarations thus
still serves every program that uses its complete parts.
