shape or holds the whole of it, or a side closed by a word other than `wall`, `cover`, `strap`, `end_stop` and `open` |
| `library.not_unit_vector` | A `dir`, `up`, or joint `axis`, a link joint's among them, that is not unit length (tolerance 0.001), or the quaternion of an environment entity's `pos` |
| `library.unsupported` | A field that exists but is not valid for this part: `collision` on a wheel, `wheel` on a sensor, `range` on a part that is not a range finder, `motor` on a part that is not a motor, `battery` on a part that is not a battery, `driver` on a part that is not a motor driver, `track` on a part that is not a track, a joint on a track's connector, a channel's current, or what the channels deliver together, on a driver without `channels`, `steering` or `driveline` outside a chassis, an `axis` on a fixed joint, a box's `size` or `origin_xyz` on a hull, a hull's `vertices` or `faces` on a box, a part's field (`inertial`, `connectors`, `profiles`, ...) on an object or an environment, `size` beside an environment entity's `ref`, `power_input` on a battery, a wheel, a track, a mount or a motor, a motor driver's `power_input` that states a voltage, `power_outputs` on a battery, a wheel, a track, a mount or a motor without a bus, a voltage or an `efficiency` beside `passes_input`, an `efficiency` on a driver without `output_voltage_v`, `ports` on a part that is not a sensor, an attachment, a chassis, a leg or a motor driver, a `role` on a UART, an Ethernet port or a bus port, a `bus` on a port of another kind, a port of kind `bus` on a motor driver, which states its buses in its `driver` block, `address` or `addresses` on a port that is not an I²C target, `links` on a part that is not a chassis, an attachment or a leg, an `axis` or a `range` on a fixed link joint, a `servo` on a fixed one, `feet` on a part that is neither used as `Legged` nor a leg, a `gait` or a `controller` on a part whose profiles do not list `Legged` or on a leg, a controller that is a policy on a chassis with no feet of its own, a foot on a cylinder, `interfaces` on a wheel, a track, a motor or a leg, `storage` on a part that is not a chassis, a mount or an attachment |
| `library.asset_missing` | `visual.file` or a controller's `policy` names a file that does not exist |
| `library.id_mismatch` | `id` differs from the directory name |
| `library.unknown_connector` | A mount names a connector the part does not declare, or a driveline or a storage region's `seat` does |
| `library.duplicate_part`, `library.part_missing` | A part registered twice, or registered without a declaration |

## Not in this version

These are needed and not yet accepted; a declaration that contains them is
rejected rather than silently ignored: a field for them with
`library.unknown_field`, a link whose parent is declared after it, a port of a kind not listed, such as `gpio`, or a 10-bit I²C
address with `library.invalid_value`, and an address on a named bus with
`library.unsupported`.

- A connector on one of a part's links (a camera on a pan-tilt's head): a
  part's connectors are in its own frame. Links that close a loop, such as a
  leg moved through a linkage.
- Shared interface types that name a hole pattern, such as goBILDA's: a name
  would not make two interfaces fit, which their holes decide.
- Slots, holes that take a fastener anywhere along them: a `holes` entry with
  a slot's `from`, `to` or `width` is `library.unknown_field`. A slot at a
  grid's site is declared by its width there, as a round hole.
- A storage region of another shape than a box square to the part frame, one
  on a part's link, a region that keeps two parts, and which of `wall`,
  `cover`, `strap` and `end_stop` comes off: a cover is not judged as removable.
- The frame of a sensor part follows REP 103: it looks along its own +x axis,
  so a mount whose `up` is the chassis' +x makes a camera look forward.
- Sensor specifications (field of view, range, rate, noise), except a range
  finder's `range` block, and a steering actuator's limits. The target still
  fills these in from its own defaults.
- A port's logic level and speed, an address on a named bus (a DYNAMIXEL id),
  a 10-bit I²C address, and command inputs by GPIO or PWM.
- Two motors on one driveline that are geared to each other, a driveline's
  losses, and how a differential shares torque when it is locked.
- A track on a steered mount, flippers, and a belt's own links and tension.
- Source tags on values other than the inertial.
- Assemblies: a part made of other parts, such as a kit, that a program places as one.
  A walker names the parts it was trained with, which a program places one by one.
- An object that moves, is pushed or opens, an object's scale, and an object
  that collides by its mesh.
- An environment placed at a pose or taken twice, one built of other
  environments, and goals or regions an environment names beside its entities.

## Changes from the previous compiler's `part.yaml`

The facts are the same; the file moved and a few names changed. A converter
belongs to the library repository.

| Was | Is | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<category>/<id>/part.yaml`, JSON text | `parts/<id>/component.yaml`, YAML | the library repository's layout; `category` is a field |
| `model` | `visual` | it is the visual model; collision and inertial are separate |
| `geometry: {radius, height}` | `wheel: {radius, width}` | says what it is |
| top-level `joint` | `connectors.<name>.joint` | the joint belongs to the mating point that creates it |
| `pos_local`, `dir_local`, `up_local` | `pos`, `dir`, `up` | every vector is in the part frame; the suffix said nothing |
| `estimate_basis` | `basis` | |
| `images`, `catalog` | not read | presentation and catalog data; the compiler no longer fails a compile because a preview image is missing |


## From the previous format

The component library repository declared its parts for the previous compiler
as `<category>/<id>/part.yaml` (`schema_version: 3`). `tools/convert-library
SOURCE DESTINATION` writes such a checkout in this format: `model` becomes
`visual` with the mesh copied under `assets/`, `pos_local`, `dir_local` and
`up_local` lose their suffix, a wheel's `geometry` becomes `wheel` (its
`height` is the `width`), the part's `joint` moves onto its connector, and
`estimate_basis` becomes `basis`. Each profile is renamed to the component
type it is (`laser` to `Lidar`, `diff_four_wheel` to `Diff_drive`, the
`arm`, `battery` and `circuit` kinds to `Attachment`), and what the compiler
never reads (`images`, `catalog`) is dropped. The converter invents nothing:
a placeholder inertial without a basis, or a steered mount whose connector
declares no kingpin, stays as it was and the loader reports it on the result.
The report of the conversion names every value it dropped or could not carry.

# Validation rules

This page is generated from `mobiledsl.validation.standard`; edit the code, not
the page. Each rule asks one question of the facts analysis derived and answers
`pass`, `fail`, `unknown` or `not_applicable` with the evidence it used. `fail`
is an error that blocks compilation, except for an advisory rule, whose `fail` is
a warning: the facts show a likely mistake that a program may still mean.
`unknown` means the facts do not settle the question; it is never a pass. The
result lists each place a rule could not decide, with what would decide it
(`undecided`), and the summary counts the rule as undecided. A place where a part
the program names does not state a fact the rule needs, or where the stated facts
leave the answer open, is usually also a warning. A place where the program has
not named a connection, or placed a part, that would decide it is listed and not
warned of, so that a program may state its mechanics before it chooses its
supplies. So is a place another rule refuses, such as a supply that comes back
round, and a fact a part does not state that the rule gives no warning for, such
as the range of a pack that states only its nominal voltage, for
`power.rated_voltage_in_supply`. A rule answers for each place it points at: one
that fails for one part and cannot decide another says both. A rule whose `fail`
column says never answers only `pass`, `unknown` or `not_applicable`: it lists
what it could not decide and refuses nothing. A rule reads facts; it does not
recompute geometry and does not change the program.

## Questions

The rules are grouped by what a person asks of a robot before building it. A check
answers each question from its rules together: `no` when a rule fails, `advised
against` when none does and an advisory rule fails, `undecided` when none fails and
one cannot decide, `yes` when every rule that applies passes, and `not judged` when
none applies. `yes` says that the rules listed here pass, on what the parts state;
it says nothing of what no rule asks.

| Question | Asks |
| --- | --- |
| assembly | Do the parts go together? |
| retention | Does each part stay where it is placed? |
| power | Does every part get its power? |
| command | Is every motor commanded, and every link joined? |
| mobility | Does the robot stand, and can it move? |
| sensing | Do its sensors see? |
| task | Can the base make the motions the task asks for? |

## Rules

| Rule | Question | Asks | `fail` is | `unknown` when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assembly.glue_on_connector` | assembly | Does every component's glue name one connector of the chassis or of a part placed on it, and is that part placed? | an error | never |
| `assembly.one_part_per_connector` | assembly | Does each chassis connector carry at most one part? | an error | never |
| `assembly.connection_placed` | assembly | Is every part placed with `on` placed: its host placed, its connections in no loop, each face pair `at` and `by` name meeting, and its place stated where its pattern, or a Mount's grid, fits the host's at more than one offset at its turn? | an error | never |
| `assembly.holes_line_up` | assembly | Does every hole of the interface a part is fastened by meet one hole of its host's, near enough for a fastener the parts state to pass both, held by any thread it meets; does a Mount fastened by its grid have two sites or more so joined to holes of its host's; and is each interface `at` names met? | an error | a hole meets one off its axis, or of another diameter, and a part does not state the fastener that would settle it, or a Mount fastened by its grid has two joined sites or more only counting sites a fastener the parts do not state would settle (a warning at that connection) |
| `assembly.one_fastener_per_hole` | assembly | Does each hole of a part take the fastener of one connection at most, whichever interface names it or a hole whose opening meets it, a Mount fastened by its grid taking every hole it is joined to? | an error | never |
| `assembly.parts_held` | retention | Is every placed part whose type can name `on`, and every part stored in a region, held where it is: fastened through the holes of a connection that fits, whose holes no earlier connection uses and no screw through three parts passes, or kept in a region closed on every side whose box holds its declared shape or explicitly selected capture feature, the first part on the region's seat; and, where it is fastened to or kept in a Mount, that Mount held too? | never | a part whose type can name `on` is glued without a declared hold, even when its part states no usable interface, or the fit of its connection is not settled or fails, or an earlier connection uses its holes too, or they would take one screw through three parts, or a side of its region is open or relies on unverified friction, its whole shape or selected capture feature reaches out of the region's box, its part declares no collision shape, or another part is on the region's seat first, or it is fastened to or kept in a Mount that is not held (listed, never warned of) |
| `assembly.wheel_mounts_filled` | mobility | Does every drive mount of the chassis type carry one wheel or track, on the mount or on the shaft of a motor on it, with any motor that turns it on the mount or on a seat of the chassis whose driveline turns it; does every other wheel mount carry one free wheel; and does nothing that drives sit elsewhere? | an error | never |
| `assembly.wheel_type_matches_chassis` | mobility | Is every wheel that rolls, and every track, of a type the chassis takes? | an error | never |
| `assembly.steering_declared` | mobility | Does each steered mount of the chassis type carry an upright kingpin? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.omni_wheels_span_the_plane` | mobility | Do an omni base's rolling directions span the plane? | an error | when no omni wheel is placed |
| `assembly.axles_horizontal` | mobility | Is the axle of every wheel that rolls, and of every track's hub, horizontal? | an error | never |
| `assembly.wheels_touch_one_plane` | mobility | Do all wheels, and both ends of every track's run, touch the ground on one plane, with each other and with a legged robot's feet (within 2 mm)? | an error | never |
| `assembly.feet_touch_the_ground` | mobility | Does every foot of a legged robot, of its chassis's own legs or of a leg placed on it, touch the ground on one plane with the others (within 2 mm), where the servos hold the legs? | an error | never |
| `assembly.legs_on_a_legged_chassis` | mobility | Is every leg placed on a Legged chassis that has no legs of its own, hanging from no connector of it that steers, and does such a chassis carry legs? | an error | never |
| `assembly.one_walker` | mobility | Is the robot, its body and its legs placed as they are, the robot of one walker of its chassis's library at most? | an error | never |
| `assembly.links_clear_the_ground` | mobility | Does every shape of a part's links but a legged robot's feet stay above the ground (within 2 mm), where its servos hold the links? | an error | no wheel, track or foot is placed |
| `statics.mass_inside_the_wheel_contacts` | mobility | Does the robot's centre of mass fall strictly inside the polygon of its ground contacts, the wheels, the tracks' runs, a legged robot's feet and the skids its parts declare, counting a skid a little above the wheels' plane once the base has tipped onto it, with no skid reaching below the wheels or the feet? | an error | no wheel, track or foot is placed, a part fastened through its holes or kept in a region is not placed, a wheel, a track's end or a foot is off the plane the others share, or the contacts lie on one line and the robot tips onto nothing declared |
| `assembly.footprint_known` | assembly | Do the parts' collision shapes, their links' with them where their servos hold them, bound the robot's footprint? | an error | a placed part declares no collision box |
| `assembly.parts_clear_each_other` | assembly | Do the declared shapes of the parts fixed to the base, each part's links' with it where their servos hold them, keep out of each other, but for what a well on a connector of either, or a storage region of either, lets into that part's declared shape? | a warning | no two shapes are found to overlap, and a placed part declares no collision shape |
| `assembly.wheels_clear_other_parts` | assembly | Does every other part's declared shape, its links' with it where their servos hold them, keep out of the space each wheel turns through, over its steering lock, and out of each track's unit, but for what a well on the part's connector or a storage region of the part lets into its declared shape? | an error | no part is found in a wheel's or a track's way, and a placed part or a track's unit declares no collision box or a stretch of a steering lock could not be settled within the analysis's budget |
| `kinematics.spin_supported` | task | If the task spins in place, can the base, and a walking base the way its gait turns? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.strafe_supported` | task | If the task strafes, is the base holonomic, and does a walking base's gait move aside to that side, as fast as the task states? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.walk_supported` | task | If the task advances, backs up or navigates a walking base, does its gait walk that way, as fast as the task states, and turn either way to navigate? | an error | never |
| `task.starts_clear_of_obstacles` | task | Where the world spawns the robot, does every part of it keep out of every obstacle, seen from above as a run is judged? | an error | no part is found in an obstacle, and a placed part declares no collision shape or a part is not placed |
| `task.goals_clear_of_obstacles` | task | At each place the task navigates to, does the disc the robot covers whichever way it faces keep out of every obstacle? | a warning | never |
| `task.speed_within_the_motors` | task | Where the task states the speed of an advance, a back-up or a strafe of a base on wheels or tracks, does it ask no driven wheel or track to move over the ground faster than it does with its motors unloaded, at the voltage their ratings hold at? | a warning | the task states such a speed, and how fast a driven wheel or track moves is not known: no motor is declared for it, a driveline states no reduction, or a track states no travel |
| `kinematics.gait_walks_the_feet` | mobility | If the chassis walks by a gait, does the robot stand on an even number of feet, four or more, each stepping by at least two servos of its own? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.tracks_state_their_travel` | mobility | Does every track's part state how far its belt travels per turn of its hub? | an error | a track's part states no travel per turn |
| `sensing.range_clears_the_ground` | sensing | Does every Range sensor's cone stay above the ground within its range? | a warning | no wheel, track or foot is placed |
| `power.loads_fed_from_a_battery` | power | Does every part the program can feed (a sensor, a motor, a motor driver, a part that states a power input or outputs, a component that names a `power`) draw its power from a battery, directly or through other parts, without the way coming back to a part it passed; and does no part that takes none name a supply? | an error | a part names no supply, a part on its way names none, or a part named as a supply states no outputs |
| `power.supply_voltage_accepted` | power | Is the voltage every part is fed, full and run down, within the range its part states it accepts? | an error | a part that states a range is fed by no battery, or its battery or output states a nominal voltage within that range and no range of its own; or a part other than a motor names no supply, or names one and states no range |
| `power.rated_voltage_in_supply` | power | Does the voltage every motor is fed, between full and run down, include the voltage its ratings hold at? | a warning | a motor is fed by no battery, or its battery or output states only a nominal voltage that is not the motor's rated one |
| `power.driver_delivers_stall_current` | power | Can every motor driver deliver, from one channel, the current the motor on it draws stalled? | a warning | never |
| `power.source_delivers_continuous_current` | power | Does every battery and power output that states the current it delivers continuously deliver what the parts behind it that are not motors draw continuously? | an error | the least the parts behind a source may draw is within its current and the most is not known or is above it: a part behind it states no current it draws, a regulator on the way states no efficiency, a voltage on the way no range or a part named as a supply no outputs, or what a regulator takes lies on both sides of the current |
| `power.source_delivers_stall_current` | power | Does every battery, power output and motor driver that states the current it delivers deliver, at its peak where its part states one, what its loads draw when every motor behind it starts at once? | a warning | the least the loads behind a source may draw as every motor starts is within its current and the most is not known or is above it: a motor may be fed above the voltage its stall current is stated at, a part behind it states no current it draws, a regulator on the way states no efficiency, a voltage on the way no range or a part named as a supply no outputs, or what a regulator, or a motor fed below its rated voltage, takes lies on both sides of the current |
| `power.source_delivers_startup_current` | power | Does every rated battery, power output and motor-driver channel group deliver, at its stated peak or otherwise continuously, what its loads draw when all loads power on together? | a warning | a load states no startup-current bound, a motor may exceed its rated voltage, a supply path lacks voltage bounds, outputs or efficiency, or the total straddles the source capacity |
| `command.driver_commands_its_motors` | command | Does every motor's driver have what commands it: a channel of its own for a motor without a bus, the motor's bus for one that carries its driver? | an error | a motor names no driver |
| `command.driver_has_a_channel_for_each_motor` | command | Does every motor driver have a channel of its own for each motor it drives? | a warning | never |
| `command.motors_on_one_channel_turn_together` | command | Do the motors that name one channel of a driver turn wheels the chassis may turn together? | an error | a motor on a channel another names is not placed, or turns no wheel or track on a mount of the chassis, and the wheels the others turn lie in one set the chassis turns together |
| `link.ports_match` | command | Does every link join two ports of one kind in complementary roles, and does no port carry more links than it takes? | an error | a sensor, or a part that states a USB device or an I²C target port, is in no link while a part states its ports or a link is named; or a part at an end of a link states no ports |
| `link.addresses_differ_on_a_bus` | command | Does every target on an I²C bus answer at addresses no other target on it answers at? | an error | a target beside others on a bus states no address, or no ports, or states only those it may be set to and its program sets none; or a link that may be I²C joins a part that states no ports, on a bus that is not known |

# Diagnostics

Every phase reports problems through one diagnostic type, defined in
`src/mobiledsl/support/diagnostics.py`. A diagnostic points at the source
bytes that caused it, says what to change, and states the facts the decision
rests on. The same object renders as a terminal line and as JSON.

## The diagnostic

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Stable identifier: two or more dotted `lower_snake_case` segments, for example `syntax.unexpected_token`, `name.duplicate`. Codes never change meaning; a changed check gets a new code. |
| `message` | One sentence naming the cause. |
| `level` | Presentation only: `error`, `warning`, `note`, `help`. |
| `phase` | The compiler phase that produced it (below). |
| `failure_domain` | Who owns the failure: `application` (the program or a library), `invocation` (command-line arguments), `environment` (files the compiler cannot read or write). |
| `base_disposition`, `effective_disposition` | Whether it blocks compilation: `blocking` or `non_blocking`. The base value is the check's own judgement; the effective value may be changed by invocation policy, and then `disposition_reason` says why. |
| `primary` | The span that caused the diagnostic, with a short label. |
| `related` | Other spans that explain it, each with a label, for example the first declaration of a duplicate name. |
| `edits` | Machine-applicable replacements, if the fix is certain. |
| `help` | What the reader should change. One short line per entry. |
| `notes` | The facts the decision rests on. One short line per entry. |

Level and blocking are independent. An `error` is normally blocking and a
`warning` normally not, but `--warnings-as-errors` changes the effective
disposition of a warning without changing its level, and the reason is
recorded on the diagnostic.

### Phases

In execution order: `source_load`, `library_load`, `target_resolution`,
`parse`, `name_resolution`, `type_check`, `analysis`, `validation`,
`target_binding`, `world_realization`, `emission`, `output_write`. Each phase
ends in one status: `pass`, `invalid`, `environment_failed`, `not_run`, or
`not_requested`.

### Codes

| Code | Phase | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invocation.unknown_source_kind`, `invocation.duplicate_source_kind`, `invocation.source_missing` | source_load | a file that is not `.core`, `.world`, `.task` or `.eval`, two files of one form, or a required form not given |
| `invocation.unknown_target`, `invocation.no_target`, `invocation.no_output`, `invocation.output_overlaps_input` | source_load | a `--target` that does not exist, `--output` without `--target` or the reverse, or an output directory that is, holds, or sits inside an input |
| `environment.source_unreadable` | source_load | a source file the compiler cannot read |
| `syntax.unexpected_token` | parse | a token no rule allows here; the message says what was expected, in plain words |
| `syntax.unexpected_character` | parse | a character that starts no token, for example `#` |
| `syntax.unexpected_eof` | parse | the source ends inside a declaration |
| `syntax.invalid` | parse | any other parser failure |
| `syntax.unknown_reference_namespace` | parse | a reference whose namespace is not `core`, `world`, or `task`; the declaration is still built |
| `syntax.number_out_of_range` | parse | a number too large for a 64-bit float, such as `1e999` |
| `syntax.duplicate_parameter` | parse | a parameter given twice in one argument list; the primary is the second occurrence and the first is related |
| `library.*` | library_load | problems in a component library; listed in [Component library format](library.md#diagnostics) |
| `name.unknown_component_type`, `name.unknown_entity_type`, `name.unknown_node_type`, `name.unknown_check` | name_resolution | a type name the vocabulary does not have; `help` suggests a near miss |
| `name.unknown_part`, `name.ambiguous_part`, `name.part_category_mismatch`, `name.type_not_supported` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a component names no part, several parts, a part of another category, an object or an environment, or a part without the type's profile; for a part of another category or without the profile, `help` lists the types the part can be used as |
| `name.unknown_object`, `name.ambiguous_object`, `name.not_an_object` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a world entity names no object or one that could not be loaded, an object several libraries have, or a part of a robot or an environment |
| `name.unknown_environment`, `name.ambiguous_environment`, `name.not_an_environment` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a scenario names no environment or one that could not be loaded, an environment several libraries have, or a part or an object. A world name the program does not declare is not reported beside it: it may be the missing environment's |
| `name.unknown_reference` | name_resolution | an `@core/`, `@world/` or `@task/` reference that nothing declares |
| `name.unknown_output`, `name.ambiguous_output` | name_resolution | an `output` that names no output of the part `power` names, `help` listing the outputs it states, or the message saying it states none; or `output` left out where that part feeds others from several, or where a motor with a bus is fed by a motor driver that states outputs, `help` listing them |
| `name.unknown_channel` | name_resolution | a motor's `channel` that names no channel of the driver its `command` names: one its part does not name, `help` listing those it names; or, on a driver whose part states only how many channels it has, a name beyond as many as it has, the message saying which motors name which |
| `name.unknown_interface`, `name.ambiguous_interface` | name_resolution | an `at` that names no interface and no storage region of the part `on` names, `help` listing those it states, or a `by` that names none of the component's own part, `help` listing those the part states; at the one name of an `at` or a `by` that lists several which names nothing; or `by` left out where the component's part states several interfaces, `help` listing those that list their holes, or, for a `Mount`, every one |
| `name.unknown_port`, `name.ambiguous_port` | name_resolution | a `port` that names no port of the part `data`, or a motor driver's `command`, names, `help` listing its ports, or the message saying it states none; or a link that several of that part's ports fit, `port` left out, `help` listing them, or that several ports of the component's own part fit, which no parameter names, `help` writing the link on the other end where one port there fits it |
| `name.duplicate` | name_resolution | two components, entities or goals with one name, or `physics`/`spawn` given twice |
| `name.chassis_missing`, `name.multiple_chassis` | name_resolution | a robot needs exactly one chassis |
| `type.unknown_parameter`, `type.missing_parameter` | type_check | an argument the type does not take, saying for `power`, `output`, `data`, `port`, `address`, `command` and `channel` on a `Mount` that a Mount has no electrical role, or a required one that is absent, or one another argument needs: `output` without the `power` whose part it names an output of, `channel` without the `command` whose driver it names a channel of, `port` or `address` without the `data`, or a motor driver's `command`, whose link they belong to, `on` without the `at` that names the interface it is fastened to or the storage region it is stored in, or `at`, `by`, `offset_m` or `turn_rad` without the `on` they qualify |
| `type.wrong_value_type`, `type.wrong_tuple_length`, `type.invalid_choice`, `type.not_positive`, `type.not_unit_vector`, `type.not_unit_quaternion` | type_check | an argument of the wrong shape or an impossible value, such as an `address` the I²C target a link joins is neither sold at nor may be set to, `help` listing those it may answer at, or a `by` that names a grid, or is left out where the component's part states grids alone, on a part that is not a `Mount`: a part is fastened by holes its interface lists, `help` saying that a part that only holds others may be a mount; or a `by` or an `offset_m` beside an `at` that names a storage region, where a part sits on the region's seat; or an `at` that lists several interfaces on a part that is not a `Mount`, a storage region among them, a name given twice or empty, or a `by` that lists neither one interface nor as many as `at` |
| `type.wrong_reference` | type_check | a reference to the wrong namespace or kind, for example `Navigate(goal = @core/...)`, or a `power` that names what can never deliver power: the component itself, a chassis, a wheel, a track, a leg, a mount, a motor without a bus, or a part that takes no power; or a `data`, or a motor driver's `command`, that names what can never be linked: the component itself, a chassis, a wheel, a track, a leg, a mount, a motor or a battery; or an `on` that names the component itself or a part that states no interfaces and no storage regions, `help` listing the components it may name |
| `type.exactly_one_of` | type_check | an entity needs one of `type`/`ref`; a goal one of `pose`/`target`; a sensor, an attachment, a mount, a battery or a motor driver one of `glue`/`on` |
| `type.size_needs_type` | type_check | an entity states `size` beside `ref`; an object has the size its library entry states |
| `type.second_ground_plane` | type_check | a scenario states `ground_plane = true` in a world that already has its floor: an environment of any of its scenarios brings one, or another scenario lays it |
| `type.part_without_interface` | type_check | a component fastened through its holes (`on`, with `at` naming an interface, or naming nothing where the program offers no storage region it could be meant for) whose own part states no interfaces, `help` naming the storage regions of the part `on` names where it could be stored instead |
| `type.object_without_collision` | type_check | an entity that collides, an `Obstacle`, a `SupportSurface` or one with `collision = true`, is made of an object that declares no collision |
| `type.children_required`, `type.children_not_allowed`, `type.one_child_required` | type_check | a composite without a child node or a task without a node, a block under an action, or a decorator without exactly one child |
| `type.bound_required`, `type.bounds_inverted` | type_check | a check without `min` or `max`, or with `min` above `max` |
| `validation.<rule>` | validation | a rule that failed (an error, or a warning for an advisory rule) or could not decide where a part does not state a fact it needs or the stated facts leave the answer open (usually a warning); a place the program has not named, or that another rule refuses, is listed above the summary and is no diagnostic ([Command line](cli.md#output)); the rules are listed in [Validation rules](validation.md) |
| `target.unsupported` | target_binding | a construct the chosen target cannot realize; [Target output](output.md) lists them |
| `target.incomplete_dynamics` | target_binding | the `mjcf` target is asked for a part with links whose mass is stated for the whole assembly, or with a joint that moves on its own and states no servo; [Target output](output.md#the-mjcf-target) |
| `target.blind_navigation` | target_binding | a warning: the task navigates, but the robot has no range sensor to feed the costmaps |
| `environment.output_unwritable` | output_write | the output directory cannot be written |
| `environment.output_linked` | output_write | a directory inside the output is a symbolic link, which the compiler does not write through |

The parser stops at the first syntax error, so a source with several syntax
errors reports one per compile. Every later phase runs over the whole input
and reports every occurrence, so one compile shows everything it can.

## Locations

A span is a half-open range of UTF-8 bytes in one source, identified by the
name the compiler was given for that source, usually its path. Spans are
exact: a diagnostic about a name covers exactly the bytes of that name.

For people, a byte offset is shown as a one-based line and a one-based
column counted in Unicode scalar values. Line terminators may be LF or CRLF.
JSON output carries both the byte offset and the line and column.

## Terminal form

The terminal form follows rustc and ruff, so a reader who knows those tools
needs no new convention:

```text
<level>[<code>]: <message>
  --> <source>:<line>:<column>
  |
N | <source line>
  |       ------ <related label>
...
M | <source line>
  |       ^^^^^^ <primary label>
  |
  = help: <what to change>
  = help: <edit message> at <source>:<line>:<column>: '<replacement>'
  = note: <fact>
  = note: <related label> at <other source>:<line>:<column>
```

The heading names the level, the code, and the cause. The arrow gives the
primary location. The excerpt shows every source line that carries a span:
the primary span is underlined with carets, related spans in the same source
with dashes, and lines with nothing to show are elided as `...`. A span that
continues onto later lines is underlined to the end of its first line; an
empty span, such as the insertion point for a missing declaration, gets one
caret. Tabs are shown as four spaces. The footer lists `help` (from `help`
and from machine edits) and `note` (from `notes`, from related spans in other
sources, from related spans beyond the first three as `and N more`, and the
reason when the effective disposition differs from the base). A span whose
source is not loaded is shown as `<source>:bytes <start>..<end>` with no
excerpt.

Color is applied when the output is a terminal. `NO_COLOR` disables it,
`FORCE_COLOR` enables it for a pipe, and `TERM=dumb` disables it; this is the
order those variables have in other CLIs. The level and the primary
underline use the level's color (`error` red, `warning` yellow, `note` cyan,
`help` green), the message is bold, and the gutter, arrows, and related
underlines are blue. Color never changes the text.

Example, a duplicate name:

```text
error[name.duplicate]: component 'wheel_lf' is declared twice
   --> demo.core:18:13
   |
17 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |             -------- first declared here
18 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (-0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |             ^^^^^^^^ declared again here
   |
```

Example, a syntax error:

```text
error[syntax.unexpected_token]: unexpected 'glue'; expected one of ')', ','
   --> demo.core:23:40
   |
23 |     Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06" glue = (0, 0.0001, 0.0344, 0, 0, 1), power = @core/reg5)
   |                                        ^^^^ not allowed here
   |
```

## JSON form

```json
{
  "code": "name.duplicate",
  "level": "error",
  "message": "component 'wheel_lf' is declared twice",
  "phase": "name_resolution",
  "failure_domain": "application",
  "disposition": {"base": "blocking", "effective": "blocking"},
  "primary": {
    "span": {
      "source": "demo.core",
      "start": {"byte_offset": 1196, "line": 18, "column": 13},
      "end": {"byte_offset": 1204, "line": 18, "column": 21}
    },
    "label": "declared again here"
  },
  "related": [
    {
      "span": {
        "source": "demo.core",
        "start": {"byte_offset": 1109, "line": 17, "column": 13},
        "end": {"byte_offset": 1117, "line": 17, "column": 21}
      },
      "label": "first declared here"
    }
  ]
}
```

This is the same diagnostic as the terminal example above.

Keys that would be empty (`related`, `edits`, `help`, `notes`) are omitted.
`disposition.reason` is present only when the effective disposition differs
from the base. An edit has `applicability` (only `machine_applicable`
exists), a `span`, a `replacement`, and an optional `message`.

## Ordering

A stream of diagnostics is sorted before it is shown or serialized, so the
output does not depend on traversal order. The key is: phase order, then
primary span (source name, start byte, end byte, label), then level, code,
message, failure domain, dispositions, then the related spans and edits.

## Machine edits

An edit replaces one span with UTF-8 text. Edits within one source must not
overlap and must not share a start offset. Applying them never mutates the
loaded sources; the result is new bytes per source. Only edits whose
correctness is certain are attached; a suggestion the author has to judge is
`help` text.

## Rules for writing a diagnostic

- Point at the bytes that caused the problem, in the program or in the part
  file. A diagnostic with no span is a last resort for environment failures.
- Name the cause in the message. Put what to change in `help` and the facts
  in `notes`; do not mix them.
- Never resolve an ambiguity for the author. Report every candidate as
  related and produce no result.
- A missing value is `unknown`, never a default; say which value is missing
  and where it is declared.
- The code is part of the interface: tests and repair tools match on it.

pages.text:
# Drive types

The chassis type decides how the base drives. It fixes the wheel mounts a program must fill, which of them drive, what the base can do, and what the targets emit to drive it.

| Chassis type | Wheels | Driven | Steered | Spins in place | Holonomic | Controller |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Diff_two_caster` | 2 `Standard`, a caster | both | none | yes | no | `diff_drive_controller` |
| `Tracked` | 2 `Track` | both | none | yes | no | the runtime's track drive |
| `Diff_drive` | 4 `Standard` | all; one motor may turn a side's two | none | yes | no | `diff_drive_controller`, two wheels a side |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | 4 `Mecanum` | all | none | yes | yes | `mecanum_drive_controller` |
| `Omni_drive` | 4 `Omni_wheel` | all | none | yes | yes | the runtime's omni drive |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | 3 `Omni_wheel` | all | none | yes | yes | the runtime's omni drive |
| `Tricycle` | 3 `Standard` | front | front | no | no | `tricycle_controller` |
| `Ackermann` | 4 `Standard` | rear, and the front pair when it is driven too; one motor may turn an axle's two | front pair | no | no | the runtime's steering drive |
| `Legged` | none: it stands on the feet of its legs, its own or `Leg` parts placed on it | its legs, on servos of their own | none | each way its gait turns | to each side its gait moves aside | the `mjcf` target's walking controller, the policy or the gait its part states; the ROS targets refuse it |

Every base the ROS targets write takes `geometry_msgs/msg/TwistStamped` on `/cmd_vel` and publishes odometry on `/odom`, whatever its controller. The controller's kinematics, wheel radius, track and wheelbase, come from the placed wheels, not from numbers you type.

## Motors

A wheel on a mount the chassis type drives is driven. Declare the motor that drives it, a `Motor` glued to the chassis like any part with the wheel glued onto its `shaft` connector, and the targets hold the wheel joint to what the motor's part states: its stall torque is the joint's effort limit and its no-load speed its velocity limit, and MuJoCo clamps the wheel's actuator to both.

```robotdsl
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0), command = @core/driver)
Standard wheel_l(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, 0.12, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
```

The motor here seats 0.02 m inside the wheel's position, and its shaft reaches out to where the wheel's glue is. A motor is declared, not required. A wheel glued straight onto a drive mount, with no motor anywhere for it, is driven as the chassis type says, within no stated limits: the kit's motors are then part of its chassis, as in every library built before motors were parts, and the output records `a wheel joint without effort or velocity limits` with the reason. A wheel glued straight onto a mount the type does not drive rolls freely, as a tricycle's rear wheels do. A motor on a mount the chassis type does not drive, a wheel beside a motor instead of on its shaft, and a motor with nothing on its shaft are each refused by `assembly.wheel_mounts_filled`.

The motor is driven by the `MotorDriver` its `command` names and fed through it by a `Battery`, both placed like any part ([Robot](../basics/robot.md#power-and-command)). Its speed and torque hold at the voltage its part states, `rated_voltage_v`, and the targets use them as they are. On a supply that never reaches that voltage, the real wheel is slower and weaker than the simulated one, and `power.rated_voltage_in_supply` warns of it.

## One motor for several wheels

A wheel need not sit on its motor's shaft. A car's axle turns both of its wheels from one motor through a differential, and a skid-steer kit often turns both wheels of a side from one motor. The chassis part says so with a `driveline` on the connector where that motor seats, naming the connectors whose wheels it turns. The program glues each wheel onto its own mount and the motor onto its seat:

```robotdsl
Ackermann chassis(ref = "car_4x4")
Motor motor_rear(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (-0.07, 0, -0.02, -1, 0, 0), command = @core/driver)
Standard wheel_rl(ref = "standard_80", glue = (-0.15, 0.13, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
Standard wheel_rr(ref = "standard_80", glue = (-0.15, -0.13, -0.02, 0, -1, 0))
```

The chassis type decides which wheels one motor may turn together: the two of a car's axle, or both axles from one driveline; the two of a skid-steer base's side; never two wheels of a mecanum or an omni base, which turns each at its own speed. The targets limit each of those wheels' joints to the motor's no-load speed over the driveline's reduction, and to an equal share of its stall torque times the reduction. A driveline that states no reduction leaves the joints without limits, and `compile.json` says so.

## What the task may ask

`Spin` needs a base that turns in place, and `Strafe` a holonomic one. The rules `kinematics.spin_supported` and `kinematics.strafe_supported` check the task against the base at compile time.

## Two-wheel and skid-steer bases

A two-wheel base turns by driving its wheels at different speeds; its caster only supports it. A skid-steer base drags its wheels sideways to turn, so the targets give its wheels less grip across their rolling direction than along it. In Gazebo the sideways grip also gives way in proportion to the sideways force, scaled alike for every wheel, so the base turns in place about its middle while every wheel carries at least half the average wheel load; one with more of its weight on an axle than that turns toward it. In MuJoCo, whose contact friction is the same in every direction, a skid-steer base turns in place at about a third of the commanded rate; the target declares this.

## Tracked bases

A `Tracked` base runs on two tracks, each driven on its own, and steers by their speed difference like a skid-steer base. A `Track` sits where a wheeled base has a wheel: on the shaft of the motor on its mount, or on the mount itself when a motor on a seat of the chassis turns it through a driveline.

```robotdsl
Tracked chassis(ref = "tracked_base")
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0.08, 0.06, -0.01, 0, 1, 0), command = @core/driver)
Track track_l(ref = "track_unit", glue = (0.08, 0.08, -0.01, 0, 1, 0))
```

A track part is the whole unit, belt, sprockets and road wheels, and states three things of its belt: how far it travels per turn of the hub the part mates by, how wide it is, and where it lies on the ground. The base's speed follows from the travel, its turning from the distance between the two runs, and its footprint and its stability from the runs themselves. The same unit turned half round serves the other side when the two motors sit at opposite ends; a unit mirrored for the other side is a part of its own.

Neither simulator models a belt's links. The targets give each track one box on its run on the ground, as wide as the belt, and the simulator moves the surface of that box: the floor's grip on it carries the base. The rest of the track unit collides with nothing. A belt is not a joint, so nothing of `ros2_control` runs for a tracked base: `runtime/run_track_drive.py` holds `/cmd_vel` to what the two belts' motors reach, each belt running at the speed of its side, hands the simulator that motion, and publishes the odometry from the two speeds.

This serves driving and navigation. It does not tell what a turn or a slope asks of a tracked robot's motors. Three things follow, each recorded in `compile.json`:

- The belts carry the base about the centre its command turns it about. A real belt runs along its track only and scrubs sideways in a turn, by an amount that follows from its pressure along the run and its grip, which a part does not state. A tracked base therefore turns as far as it is commanded here, and its odometry agrees with where it is.
- A belt takes a speed, not a force: it is held to the speed its motor reaches unloaded, and its pull is bounded by the floor's grip, not by the motor's stall torque.
- A belt's hub does not turn, so `Check_vel`, `Check_acc`, `Check_jerk` and `Check_effort` on a `Track` are refused at compile time.

The two tracks lie equally far to the two sides of the chassis part's origin; a chassis whose origin is not midway between its track mounts is refused.

## Steering bases

A tricycle or an Ackermann base steers its front wheels about kingpins. The chassis part states each steered mount's kingpin axis and how far it turns:

```yaml
wheel_mount_front:
  pos: [0.15, 0, -0.02]
  dir: [0, 1, 0]
  steering: {axis: [0, 0, 1], max_angle_rad: 0.6}
```

The targets hang the part on that mount, the motor of a driven wheel or a free wheel itself, from a light knuckle that turns about that axis, and plan with Smac Hybrid-A* at the base's minimum turning radius, following the path with MPPI's Ackermann model. That radius is the tightest circle the kingpins allow: a kingpin a wheelbase ahead of the rear axle and some way off the centre line holds the turn that has it on the inside to the wheelbase over the tangent of its limit, plus that distance. A steering base is not held to a final heading, since it cannot turn in place to correct one, and it cannot `Spin`.

An Ackermann base drives its rear wheels and may drive its front wheels too, both or neither: with a motor on each steered mount and the wheel on its shaft, or with a motor on a seat whose driveline turns the two front hubs. Both targets drive every wheel the program drives. ros2_controllers' Ackermann controller takes exactly two traction joints, so the runtime's steering drive stands in its place for every car: it turns `/cmd_vel` into the speed of each driven wheel along its own circle about the turning centre and the angle of each kingpin, and takes the odometry from the measured speeds of the rear wheels. In a turn the front wheels travel further than the rear ones and are driven that much faster.

## Omni bases

An omni wheel grips along its rolling direction and slides along its axle. The runtime's omni drive turns `/cmd_vel` into each wheel's speed from its position and rolling direction, and computes the odometry back from the measured wheel speeds. That works for any layout, including the rectangles most four-wheel omni bases are built on, as long as the wheels' rolling directions span the plane; the rule `kinematics.omni_wheels_span_the_plane` checks that.

## Mecanum bases

A mecanum wheel's rollers let it slide along one diagonal. In Gazebo, each wheel is a sphere that grips along one diagonal and slides along the other. MuJoCo cannot yet model that sliding, so the `ros-mujoco-nav2` target refuses mecanum and omni bases.

[Chassis types](../../reference/vocabulary.md#chassis-types) in the vocabulary lists the mounts of each type.

pages.text:
# Sensors

A sensor is a part placed like any other; its component type says what the targets simulate and what navigation does with its data.

| Type | Publishes | Feeds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Lidar` | `/scan` | The costmaps and the localizer |
| `Lidar3D` | `/lidar3d/points`, its middle ring on `/lidar3d/scan` | The costmaps; the ring stands in for a laser |
| `DepthCamera` | `/depth/image_raw`, `/depth/points` | The costmaps; a scan made from its cloud stands in for a laser |
| `RGBD` | `/rgbd/image_raw`, `/rgbd/depth/image_raw`, `/rgbd/points`, `/rgbd/camera_info` | As for a depth camera |
| `Camera` | `/camera/image_raw`, `/camera/camera_info` | Nothing; the images are yours |
| `IMU` | `/imu` | Nothing; the readings are yours |
| `Ultrasonic` | `/ultrasonic/range` | The costmaps' range layer |
| `Range` | `/range` | The costmaps' range layer |
| `Bumper` | `/bumper`, the contacts it feels | `Check_contact` |

The first sensor of a type gets these topics; a second one of the same type is suffixed with its component name. Each sensor's frame is its component name.

## Which sensor navigation uses

Nav2's costmaps mark what every point cloud sees, between 0.05 and 2 m above the ground. The costmaps and the localizer also read one planar scan, chosen in this order:

1. the first `Lidar`;
2. the middle ring of the first `Lidar3D`;
3. a scan made from the first depth or RGBD camera's cloud, projected onto the ground plane.

A range finder's reading marks the costmaps' range layer. A robot with no range sensor at all is warned that it navigates blind.

## Range finders

`Ultrasonic` measures with sound, `Range` with light: an infrared triangulation sensor or a time-of-flight one. Both report the nearest thing in a narrow cone along their `+x`, as `sensor_msgs/Range`, and differ in what the floor does. A sound pulse glancing off the floor does not come back, so an ultrasonic sensor's floor returns are dropped. Light does come back from a matte floor, so a `Range` sensor reads the floor wherever its cone meets it within its range, and the costmaps then mark the floor as an obstacle. The rule `sensing.range_clears_the_ground` warns about such a sensor at compile time and says how far to tilt it up, or how high to mount it.

A `Range` part states what it measures, from its maker's datasheet, in a `range` block: `min_m`, `max_m`, `field_of_view_rad` and `rate_hz`. A sensor that says only whether something is within one distance states that distance as both `min_m` and `max_m`; it reports `-inf` when something is there and `+inf` when nothing is, as `sensor_msgs/Range` defines it, and the range layer marks or clears its cone. An `Ultrasonic` part may state a `range` block too.

## Specifications the targets fill in

Except for a range finder's `range` block, a library part does not yet state a sensor's specification: its range, beam count, field of view or rate. Until it does, the targets use these, and declare each one in `compile.json`:

| Type | Simulated as |
| --- | --- |
| `Lidar` | 360 beams over the full circle, 0.3 to 12 m, 10 Hz |
| `Lidar3D` | 16 rings of 360 beams over 0.52 rad, 0.3 to 20 m, 10 Hz |
| `Camera` | 320 by 240 pixels, 1.089 rad field of view, 10 Hz |
| `DepthCamera`, `RGBD` | 160 by 120 pixels, 1.089 rad field of view, depth 0.1 to 5 m, 10 Hz |
| `IMU` | Ideal, 100 Hz |
| `Ultrasonic` | A cone of 9 by 9 beams, 0.52 rad, 0.02 to 4 m, 20 Hz unless the part states its own; the nearest return more than 0.05 m above the ground is the reading |
| `Range` | A cone of 9 by 9 beams over the part's stated cone, range and rate; the nearest return is the reading, the floor included |
| `Bumper` | An ideal contact switch over its collision box, 50 Hz |

## Mounting

A sensor looks along its own `+x`. The connector it is glued to, of the chassis or of a part placed on it, together with the connector's `up`, decides which way that points on the robot; the TF tree carries the result, so a sensor mounted upside down still reports correctly in its own frame.
